Its opening with "Praise be to God" (al-hamdu lillah) indicates that attributes of God's majesty will be mentioned in it. The application of action-attributes to the Name of Majesty (Allah), through His creating the heavens and the earth and the best of what is in them, namely the angels and the messengers, indicates that the surah came to establish monotheism (tawhid) and to affirm the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). The indication of "Praise be to God" that God alone deserves it, to the exclusion of any other, has already been discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Fatiha.

Al-fatir is the agent noun of fatr, which means creation. It carries the sense of bringing into being swiftly, because it is derived from fatr, which means splitting. From this usage come God's words ﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from above them﴾ [al-Shura: 5] and ﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ [al-Infitar: 1]. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I did not know what 'Fatir of the heavens and the earth' meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who fatartuha (initiated it).'" That is, "I began it." I think that the description of God as ﴿Fatir of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 14] is among the things the Qur'an was the first to use. It was discussed under His words ﴿Fatir of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 14] in Surat al-An'am, and under His words ﴿You have taught me something of the interpretation of events, Fatir of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yusuf: 101] at the end of Surat Yusuf. Add it to what is here.

As for jā'il, it is used in the sense of "creator" (mukawwin) and in the sense of "one who makes into" (musayyir). According to each of these two senses, the position of His words "messengers" (rusulan) differs. It may be a second object of jā'il, meaning that God made from among the angels (for them to be messengers from Him, to do what He wills by their own inherent power). Or it may be a circumstantial state (hal) of the angels, meaning that He makes it part of their condition that they be sent. Because both meanings are suitable, the root j-‘-l was chosen rather than conjoining it to the object of fatir.

The singling out of the angels from among the creatures of the heavens and the earth is due to their nobility, since they are the inhabitants of the heavens, and to the magnificence of their creation.

He attached to them the attribute that they are messengers, in keeping with the purpose of establishing the messengership, meaning: the one who makes them messengers from Him to the human messengers, for the purpose of revelation, with what is to be conveyed by them to people.

His words ﴿possessors of wings﴾ may be a circumstantial state of the angels, in which case the wings are inherent to them, among the constituents of their creation. Or it may be a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "messengers," in which case it refers specifically to their state of being messengers.

Ajniha is the plural of janah (wing), with a fatha on the jim. It is what a bird has in the place of a human's hand. It is possible that the affirmation of wings for the angels in this verse, and in some hadiths narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), is literal. It is also possible that it is a metaphor for the power by which they traverse the heavenly horizons upward and downward, whose true nature none knows but God Most High.

"Mathna" and its counterparts are words indicating repetition of number names. They are derived starting from two, with the form mathna, then three and four with the forms thula and ruba'. Most often, they do not go beyond the number four with this form, though it is said they may go up to ten. The meaning is "two by two," etc. His words ﴿to stand before God, in pairs and singly﴾ [Saba': 46] were discussed in Surat Saba'.

The discussion of "ulī" has already been given.

The meaning is: they possess wings, some of which are arranged in pairs, two by two in a row, some in threes, and some in fours. This can multiply in rows to reach large numbers. Therefore, this does not contradict what is reported in the hadith from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet (ﷺ) "saw Jibril having six hundred wings."

It is possible that the numbers of wings vary for each angel at different times, according to the distances they are commanded to traverse through the heavens and the earths. The more evident view is that wings are among the states of the forms in which the angels take shape. In the narration of al-Zuhri, Jibril said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you were to see Israfil, he has twelve thousand wings, and the Throne rests upon his shoulder."

Know that the reality of the angels is summarized in what Sa'd al-Din (al-Taftazani) mentioned in his book al-Maqasid: "They are subtle, luminous bodies (ajsam latifa nurraniyya), able to take forms of various shapes; their disposition is goodness and obedience, knowledge, and the ability to perform arduous tasks; their dwelling is the heavens." He said: "This is the apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunna, and it is the view of most of the Community." End of quote. The meaning of "subtle bodies" is that they belong to the category of jawhar (substance) and not 'arad (accident), and that they are substances of what the philosophers call mujarrad (immaterial beings).

In my view, al-Maqasid's definition of the reality of the angels is not free from confusion in the order of the definition, because in it he mixed essential attributes (dhatiyyat) with accidental attributes ('aradiyyat).

In my view, the correct order of the definition is to say: subtle, luminous bodies, good, possessing great strength, and among their distinctive features are the ability to take various forms, knowledge of what their works depend upon, and their abode is the heavens, so long as they have not been sent to a region of the earth.

This taking of form is a contraction and condensing of the particles of their luminosity and giving their essence a form from the forms of dense corporeal things. What indicates their taking form is God's words to them on the day of Badr ﴿Strike above the necks and strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. It is also established that Jibril (peace be upon him) took the form of Dihya al-Kalbi for the Prophet (ﷺ), and that he took a form for him and for 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in the "Hadith of the Questioning about faith, Islam, excellence, and the Hour," in the form of a man with exceedingly white clothes and exceedingly black hair, on whom no trace of travel was visible, and none of us, meaning of the people of Madina, knew him, until he sat before the Prophet (ﷺ), leaned his knees against his knees, and placed his palms on his thighs. [The hadith continues.] And there is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying after the man had departed from them: "Do you know who the questioner was?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "It was Jibril; he came to you to teach you your religion." This is in the Two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. It is also established that Jibril descended to the cave of Hira' at the beginning of revelation, and that he appeared to the Prophet (ﷺ) on a throne between heaven and earth in the form in which he had seen him in the cave of Hira', as is in the hadith about the revelation of Surat al-Muddaththir. And many of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw on the day of Badr men they did not recognize, on horses, fighting alongside them.

His words ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ form a resumed clause (istinaf bayani), an explanatory resumption, because the mentioned attributes of the angels arouse the listener's wonder, so that he asks about this wondrous attribute. He is answered by this resumption: the will of God Most High is not confined or limited in time. Each kind of created being has its constituents and distinctive properties. So "creation" here means all created beings, meaning that God increases in some of them what He does not give to another creation. This includes the increase in the strength of some angels over others, and every increase in something among created beings of virtues and excellences: soundness of intellect, beauty of form, courage, eloquence of tongue, and fluency of speech. It is also possible that the clause ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ is a second attribute of the angels, meaning: possessors of wings, two, three, or four, He increases in their creation what He wills, as if it were said: two, three, four, or more. Thus what is in some hadiths about the multitude of Jibril's wings clarifies the meaning of ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾. In this case, "creation" means what the angels were created with, namely that some of them have additional wings beyond what others have.

The clause ﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾. In this there is an allusion to deriding the minds of those who denied messengership and said ﴿You are only human like us﴾ [Ibrahim: 10]. They were answered with the words of the messengers: ﴿We are only human like you, but God bestows favor upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [Ibrahim: 11].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 2:

﴿Whatever mercy Allah opens for mankind, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ This is part of the continuation of the opening of the surah with ﴿Praise be to Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1], and it is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿Creator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1], etc. The implied sense is: "and the Opener of mercy to mankind and the Withholder of it from them; so none can withhold what He has opened, nor open what He has withheld."

The "mā" here is conditional (sharṭiyyah), that is, a noun containing the meaning of a condition. Its origin is a relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl) which was given the meaning of a condition. Its relative clause was thus transformed into a conditional clause, and the predicate clause became the response (jawāb), and it is therefore joined by the particle "fa" (then). Thus the origin of the conditional "mā" is the relative "mā." The position (maḥall) of "mā" is the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the response of the condition takes the place of the predicate (khabar).

"﴿Min raḥmah﴾" (of mercy) is an explanation (bayān) of the vagueness of "mā," and the returning pronoun (rābiṭ) is omitted because it is an object pronoun in the accusative.

"Al-fatḥ" (opening) is a metaphorical depiction (tamthīliyyah) for the giving of mercy, since mercy is among the precious things resembling stored treasures that people compete for. Thus Allah's giving of mercy resembles the state of opening treasuries for bestowal. This depiction is indicated by the verb "opening," and its explanation by the phrase "﴿of mercy﴾" is the indicator (qarīnah) of the metaphorical allegorical figure (al-istiʿārah al-tamthīliyyah).

Al-imsāk (withholding), its literal meaning is: taking a thing with the hand while gripping it tightly, lest it fall or slip away, and it is transitive by itself. Or it is here a metaphor for confining and preventing, and for this reason "opening" is contrasted with it.

As for the people's saying "amsaka bi-kadhā" (he held on to such-and-such), the "bā'" is either to emphasize the adherence of the object to its verb, as in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and do not hold onto the ties of disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], or it is to imply the meaning of "iʿtiṣām" (holding fast), as in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256].

People have been misled in al-Qamus, al-Lisan and al-Taj into thinking that it is not transitive by itself.

So His statement here, ﴿and whoever withholds﴾, has its object omitted, indicated by His statement ﴿whatever mercy Allah opens for mankind﴾ upon it. The implied sense is: "and whoever withholds it of mercy." No explanation was mentioned for it, being sufficed by its explanation from the verb.

Al-irsāl (sending/releasing) is the opposite of al-imsāk (withholding). The transitivity of "irsāl" with the preposition "lām" is for reinforcement, because the operating element here is a branch in its function.

And "﴿min baʿdihi﴾" (after Him) means "min dūnihi" (other than Him), as in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿so who can guide him after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23] and ﴿then in what message after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 6]; that is: "there is no releaser for it apart from Allah," meaning no one can nullify what Allah wills of giving or withholding. ﴿And Allah judges; there is no repealer of His judgment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. The masculine form of the pronoun in His statement ﴿so there is no releaser for it﴾ observes the wording of "mā," since it has no explanation attached; and its feminine form in His statement ﴿so there is no withholder of it﴾ observes the explanation of "mā" in His statement "﴿of mercy﴾," because it is nearer.

The coordination of ﴿and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) in which the aspect of information was preferred, so it was coordinated. The apparent requirement would have been for it to be disjoined, to convey that He opens and withholds for a wisdom that He knows, and that no one can undo what He has firmly decreed concerning the opening of mercy and His other dispositions, because Allah is Almighty; it is not possible for anyone to overcome Him. Undoing what has been firmly decreed is a form of humiliation and abasement. For this reason, it was among the emblems of the lord of nobility that he firmly decrees and undoes. Al-A'sha said:

"ʿAlqama, you are not one to the Amir, the one who undoes the bowstrings and the avenger."

The pronoun "lahā" (its) and the pronoun "lahu" (its) both refer to "mā" in His statement ﴿whatever mercy Allah opens for mankind﴾. The feminine form of one of the two pronouns observed the meaning of "mā," since it is a noun that applies to "raḥmah" and has been explained by it; and the masculine form of the other pronoun observed the wording of "mā," since it is a wording with no feminine marker. These are two common considerations in such cases in eloquent speech, so the speaker has the choice between whichever of the two considerations he wishes. Combining them in this verse is a stylistic variation (tafannun). The feminine pronoun referring to "mā" was preferred because it is explained by a feminine expression, namely "min raḥmah."

**"O mankind, remember the favour of God upon you. Is there any creator other than God who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?"** When the mention of God's mercy, which encompasses all people, had come, He turned to address them, [urging them] to remember God's particular favour upon them, the favour that is specific to each one individually. From these particular favours the general mercy for all people is composed, and these are only part of God's mercy toward His creatures.

The purpose of remembering the favour is to be grateful for it and to appreciate it at its proper worth. Among the greatest of these favours is the favour of the Muhammadan message (risalah), which is the means by which those people who follow it attain eternal bliss. Here, remembrance (dhikr) means remembering with the heart and with the tongue. It is either an instance of the homonym (al-mushtarak, a word with multiple meanings) being used in its general sense, or it is the use of the shared common meaning, since remembrance by the tongue and remembrance by the heart imply one another; otherwise the first would be mere babbling and the second mere concealment. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Better than remembrance of God by the tongue is remembrance of God at His commands and His prohibitions," meaning that there is merit in both.

The favour is described with **"upon you"** (ʿalaykum) because the intended remembrance is the kind that leads to gratitude, not mere remembrance in the sense of reflection and contemplation on the wondrous bounty of God. That latter has another context. Moreover, His saying **"Is there any creator other than God who provides for you?"** already includes a call to consider the evidence for God's oneness (tawhid), power and bounty.

The interrogative is denunciatory (inkari), meaning negation. For this reason what follows it is joined with **"min"**, which is added to emphasise the negation. The interrogative particle **"hal"** was chosen over the hamzah (the particle alif-hamzah) because of what is inherent in the meaning of **"hal"** of indicating confirmation and affirmation, since it is originally in the sense of **"qad"** and conveys emphasis of negation.

Because of the importance of this exception, it is placed in the discourse before what is in effect the thing excepted. It is made a qualifier of **"khaliq"** (creator), since **"ghayr"** (other than) is suitable for both considerations. For this reason the well-known recitations treat **"ghayr"** here as a qualifier of **"khaliq"**. The majority of reciters read **"ghayr"** with a nominative ending (ghayru), on the basis that the position of **"khaliq"**, which is in the genitive after **"min"**, is nominative as a subject. The nominative is not visible because of the vowel of the redundant preposition. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read it with the genitive (ghayri), following the wording rather than the grammatical position. Both are eloquent usages in such constructions, and Sibawayh drew attention to them in his book.

The clause **"yarzuqukum"** (who provides for you) may be a second qualifier of **"khaliq"**, and it may also be an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'nafan bayaniyyan).

The negation is directed at the qualifying clause, which is the descriptive clause, as is its established practice in restricted statements. This is because the aim is to remind people of God's favours so that they may give thanks. This amounts to an implicit argument (kinayah) for the negation of the attribute of creation from anyone other than Him, since if anyone other than Him were a creator, he would also be a provider. Creation without provision is deficient as creation, because a created being without provision will inevitably come to ruin and non-existence, and so its creation would be vain. This is something to be exalted above in the one who is described with divinity, which requires wisdom. Thus the verse reminds [people] of the two favours: bringing into existence and sustaining.

The addition of **"from the heaven and the earth"** is a reminder of the multiplicity of sources of provision. Some of them are from the heavens, such as rain, from which comes drink and purification, and which is the cause of the growth of trees and herbage; such as the manna that descends upon particular trees from dews in the atmosphere; such as light from the sun, guidance by the stars at night; and likewise the kinds of birds that are hunted. All of these are from the heaven.

From the earth come many provisions: grains, fruits, oils, fruits of various kinds, minerals, herbage, truffles, and fish of seas and rivers.

There is another benefit in this qualification, namely to repel the misconception of the heedless that provisions come to them from other than God, in the form of gifts that some people give to others and exchanges that some people conduct with one another. Because these are so frequently circulated among them, occupation with them may distract them from reflecting on the origins of their sources, since the origins of their materials are the handiwork of God. Thus what people receive from them ultimately comes from God, in the manner of the case of the one who disputed with Abraham concerning his Lord, when Abraham said to him, **"My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." He said, "I give life and cause death."** This man was [like someone who says]: "Here is a man sentenced to death; behold, I pardon him, and so I have given him life; and here is a living man; behold, I order him to be executed, and so I cause him to die." Abraham then moved on to say to him, **"Indeed God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."**

**"There is no deity except Him; so how are you deluded?"**

This is a conclusion following the mention of the evidence, since the sole possession of creation and provision is made the basis for His sole possession of divinity, because these two attributes are the clearest signs of divinity among people. Therefore the clause **"There is no deity except Him"** is a new independent statement. Following it comes the expression of wonder at their turning away from considering the evidences of oneness, by the clause **"so how are you deluded?"**

**"Anna"** is an interrogative noun that comes with the meaning of asking about a state, a place or a time. The interrogation here is specifically about the state of their turning away, and it is used in the sense of wonder at their turning away from acknowledging oneness, following those who turn them away, who are their protectors and their elders.

**"Tu'fakun"** (you are deluded/turned away) is in the passive voice, from **"afaka"** in the pattern of **"daraba"**, meaning to turn someone away and divert him. The one who is turned away is "ma'fuk." The agent is omitted here because those who turn them away are many kinds of people. This was already mentioned in the words of God, **"God fight them! How are they deluded?"** (Tawbah 9:30), in the surah "Bara'ah."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 4:

﴿And if they deny you, [know that] messengers before you were denied, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾ [Fatir: 3], meaning: and if they persist in turning away from accepting your call and do not give thanks for the favour of being sent to them, then there is no cause for wonder, for peoples before them denied messengers before [you].

This is a shift from addressing the people to addressing the Prophet ﷺ, because the address to the people was being conducted through his tongue; he is therefore a witness to their address, and it is fitting that the address be directed to him after it was directed to them, since the situation is one. Similar is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and [you, wife], ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 29].

Since He had made clear to them the proof of Allah's exclusive divinity when He addressed them with that, the report concerning the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ was conveyed in respect of what they denied accepting from him. For when his truthfulness in that matter had been established by proof, it was fitting that those who denied him be presented with the same outcome as those who denied the messengers before him. Within this is woven consolation to the Messenger ﷺ over his people's denial of him, that his station in this was no lower than the station of the earlier messengers.

In this conditional the particle ﴿in﴾ (in) is used, whose original function is to attach a condition whose occurrence is not certain. This treats them, after the proof of Allah's oneness that confirms what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought them had been presented to them, and they denied him in it, as one who has certainty of the Messenger's truthfulness. Thus the supposition of their persistence in denying him is only posed as one posits the impossible.

This is the reason for choosing the conditional here with the present-tense verb within the conditional clause, which becomes specific to the future: i.e., if denial occurs from them after the decisive proofs have struck their ears.

What is stated as the answer to the condition is in fact the cause of an omitted answer, the implied sense being: "And if they deny you, then let their denial not grieve you, since messengers before you were denied," so the cause is mentioned in place of the effect, as it indicates it.

"Messengers" (rusul) is not made definite but is given in indefinite form, because indefiniteness carries the indication of magnifying those messengers, in addition to the aspect of the attribute of messengership, in respect of their number and the variety of the signs of their truthfulness, and yet their peoples denied them.

Coordinated with this consolation and allusion is what serves as an emphasis for both and a reminder of the outcome of their content: that the matter of the deniers has come to their meeting as recompense for their denial, from the One to whom all matters are returned. So the matter of those deniers and the matter of those messengers fall within the general category of matters returned to Allah, Exalted is He, since their affairs do not leave the scope of the general matters.

This sentence has acquired the meaning of a concluding summation (tadhyil) through the generality it contains.

"Al-umur" (the matters): the plural of amr, which means affair or condition, i.e., all conditions are returned to Allah, who disposes of them as He wills. Thus the verse is a threat to the deniers and a warning.

The address to people is repeated as a warning and admonition to them, and to affirm that God's promise, which He made of His punishment for those who deny (Him) on the Day of Resurrection, is a promise that will certainly come to pass and will not fail. This comes after he has presented them with a reminder of the proofs of divine oneness (tawhid) that it contains, together with an indication of God's blessings upon them, so that they may know that none other than Him deserves worship and that none other than Him truly possesses divinity (ilahiyya).

After he has pointed out to them that what those proofs produce is what the Messenger ﷺ informed them of, so that they may know his truthfulness in what he told them about God's oneness, which is the greatest matter to strike their ears and the most painful thing to their souls. When this is confirmed by a demonstrative proof (burhani), the way is prepared for accepting the Messenger's ﷺ truthfulness in what he informed them of concerning God's promise, which is the Day of Resurrection. For once his truthfulness has been made clear in the first matter, his truthfulness in the second is known by the reasoning of equal analogy (qiyas al-musawat).

The address is either to the polytheists, or to them and to the believers, because what follows is suitable for admonishing both groups, each according to its condition.

The emphasis of the statement with "inna" is either because the address is to those who deny, or to give precedence to the group of deniers over the believers, since they are in greater need of strengthening the admonition.

"Al-wa'd" (promise) is a verbal noun, meaning the report of the speaker's action regarding something in the future. Most often it is used for what is other than evil, while evil is specifically called "al-wa'id" (threat). The term covers both, and here it is used in the common sense shared by both. This was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:268], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Its attribution to the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam, i.e. Allah) is a preparation for it being true, because falsehood does not come from God.

Here "al-haqq" (the true) is the opposite of falsehood. The meaning is: God's promise is truthful. Describing it by the verbal noun is an intensification of its truthfulness.

What is meant by it is the promise of the arrival of a day of recompense after the end of this life, as indicated by the consequence stated in ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾ and what follows.

"Al-ghurur" with a damma on the ghayn, and it is said "al-taghrir," means: presenting harm and corruption as benefit and goodness. This was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Let not the strutting of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:196], in Surat Ali 'Imran, and at His saying, ﴿ornamented speech as a deception﴾ [al-An'am 6:112], in Surat al-An'am.

What is meant by "al-hayat" (life) is what the conditions of the worldly life contain of frivolity and luxury, and its ending in death and nonexistence, which makes people imagine that there is no other life after this one.

Attributing the deception to "al-hayat" (life), even with an implied modifier, is a metaphorical attribution, because the one who deceives a person is his own self, which is deceived by the conditions of the worldly life. So it is the attribution of the act to its cause and what prompts it.

The prohibition, outwardly, is directed at people, while what is forbidden is among the conditions of the worldly life. Since the worldly life is not a human act, it becomes clear that the intended meaning is a prohibition against the necessary consequence of that attribution, which is being deceived by the outward appearances of life. A similar usage is common in Arabic speech, such as their saying: "I shall not know you doing such-and-such," and "I shall not see you here," and ﴿And let not the hatred of a people lead you into transgression﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:2]. Its like was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Let not the strutting of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ at the end of Ali 'Imran.

The same applies to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning God.﴾

As for "al-Ghurur" with a fatha on the ghayn, it is one who is very effective in deceiving. What is meant by it is the Shaytan, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he caused them to fall by deception﴾ [al-A'raf 7:22]. He deceives people by adorning their ugly deeds for them, disguising them with the appearance of goodness that suits human souls.

The "ba'" in His saying "﴿bi-Allah﴾" is for association (mulabasa), and it is attached to an implied omitted noun, meaning: "concerning the matter of God," i.e., it extends to undermining God's guidance. For the verb "gharra" is transitive to one object, and when it is intended to be transitive to some of its complements, it is made transitive by means of a particle of genitive, so it may be transitive with "ba'," which is the "ba'" of association, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ [al-Infitar 82:6], and His saying in Surat al-Hadid, ﴿and the Deceiver deceived you concerning God﴾ [al-Hadid 57:14]. This is when it is intended to specify the one with whom the Deceiver is associated, with an implied noun, meaning: a condition of His. That is the association of the verb with the object in concise speech. This "ba'" is not the "ba'" of causation.

The verse contains two kinds of deception: a deception that a person falls into from his own self, and which he adorns for himself out of the captivating appearances that show themselves to him in this world, so that he imagines them to be good and does not look at their consequences, such that their harms are hidden at first sight, and he does not suspect that they come from the Shaytan.

And a deception that he receives from the one who deceives him, who is the Shaytan. Likewise, all deception in this world is of two kinds: some of it a person suggests to his own self, and some of it he receives from the devils of mankind and jinn. The detailed explanation of the first deception is left aside for now, out of concern for what is fundamental and more important, since every deception returns to the deception of the Shaytan. Its detailed explanation will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whoever desires honour, then to God belongs all honour﴾ [Fatir 35:10].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 6:

Page 260

﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party so that they may become among the companions of the Blaze.﴾ Since in His words ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾ [Fatir: 5] there was an ambiguity regarding what is meant by "the Deceiver" (al-gharur), this was followed by its clarification, that the Deceiver is Satan, so that the predicate would be established through the explanation after the ambiguity. Thus the clause ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾ stands in the position of an explanation (bayan) relative to what is explained (mubayyan) in the clause ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾ [Fatir: 5]. For this reason it is disconnected and not conjoined by a conjunction. This is one of the indications of the arrangement of speech according to the intention of the speaker, since the listener knows from the mention of the attribute of Satan immediately after the attribute of deception that the Deceiver is Satan.

The name Satan is made explicit in a place where a pronoun would be expected, to make clear that what is meant by the Deceiver is Satan. Stirring up enmity between people and Satan is one of the meanings of the Qur'an, both explicitly and implicitly, and here it is explicit, as in His words ﴿And We said: Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36].

This enmity is deposited in his nature, like the enmity of the dog toward the cat, because Satan's nature is entrusted with bringing people into corruption and the worst consequences in embellished and adorned forms. Evidence of this appears to a person in himself and in events wherever he finds it. Allah the Exalted has said ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 27].

The emphasis of the statement with the particle of emphasis (inna) is for the purpose of affirming it, because people, through their heedlessness of Satan's enmity, are like one who denies that Satan is an enemy.

The fronting of "lakum" (to you) before its complement is for the sake of giving importance to this complement, and from it is derived the command to take him as an enemy, because when they know that he is an enemy to them, it is incumbent upon them to take him as an enemy; otherwise they would be in folly. In this there is also an alert to the obligation of opposing those who call to misguidance and who draw their strength from Satan.

The discussion of the word "enemy" (ʿaduww) has preceded at His words ﴿So if he was from a people who are enemies to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 92] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The lam in "lakum" is the lam of specification (lam al-ikhtisas), which is what the idafa (genitive construction) implies. Since he placed first what should have been the mudaf ilayh (the second term of the construction), he made the lam explicit so that the meaning of the idafa would be achieved.

Page 261

Allah commanded taking the enemy as an enemy and did not recommend pardoning him or overlooking his enmity, as He commanded in His words ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and similar things that are repeated in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Messenger ﷺ. This is because what is recommended of pardon applies only among Muslims with one another, hoping for the improvement of the enemy's condition, since a Muslim's enmity is incidental, arising from motives that can cease, and it has limits beyond which grave harms are not feared, as He the Exalted said ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. For this reason Allah the Exalted did not command the like of this with the enemies of the religion, so He said ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and so on. Rather, Allah the Exalted did not command pardon for those who wage war from among the people of the religion, because their hostility is not incidental, but is for the purpose of seizing wealth and the like, so He said ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 34]. Thus, since the enmity of Satan is innate, with no hope of its ceasing even if one pardons him, Allah commanded only taking him as an enemy, because if he is not taken as an enemy, the Muslim will not guard against his schemes and deceptions. Among the necessary consequences of taking him as an enemy is acting contrary to what he calls to, in order to avoid his schemes and out of hatred for him through righteous action.

Bringing people into harm does not spare his allies or his enemies, but his allies he secretly harbors enmity toward, and he is at ease with them, because he achieves his aim through them. As for his enemies, despite his enmity toward them, he recoils, flees, and is enraged at their resistance to his whisperings, to the point of fleeing from the great ones of the Ummah. The Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUmar: «Ah, O son of al-Khattab, Satan has never seen you walking a path but he has taken a different path from yours.» It is recorded in the Sahih: «When the prayer is established, Satan turns his back» [and so on]. It is also reported that «Satan was never seen more humiliated, more belittled, than on the Day of 'Arafah, because of what he sees of mercy.»

The command to take Satan as an enemy is followed by a warning against accepting his call and an exhortation to the obligation of vigilance against his deception and to avoiding alliance with him, by stating that he strives to harm his allies and party, so he calls them to what casts them into the Blaze. This reinforces the command to take him as an enemy, because the people most harmed by him are his party and his allies.

The clause ﴿He only invites his party so that they may become among the companions of the Blaze﴾ is a causal explanation of the clause ﴿so take him as an enemy﴾. It is given in the form of restriction (qasr), to confine his call to the stated end that follows it with the lam of cause, lest it be supposed that his call might be free of that end even at some time.

Page 262

With this generality which restriction implies, the clause also comes to have the sense of a concluding summary (tadhyil) for everything preceding it.

The consequence of the verb "yad'u" (invites) falling within the scope of restriction is that its object, which is "hizbahu" (his party), is the intended focus of the restriction, meaning: he invites his party and does not invite others than his party. Satan invites all people alike, including his party and those who do not incline to his call; but the effect of his call appears only in those who incline to him, and they become his party. Allah the Exalted said ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], and Allah related the words of Satan ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82] ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad: 83]. Thus it is established that in the speech there is an elliptical omission (ijaz hadhf). The estimated meaning is: He only invites his party with a call that reaches its aim. The indication is what preceded of warning; for if he invited only his party, there would be no benefit in warning others.

The lam in His words ﴿so that they may become among the companions of the Blaze﴾ may be the lam of cause, since Satan may indeed be striving for the aim of casting the children of Adam into punishment, out of spite toward them, and this is a cause of the call that is hidden in his satanic intention, even though he does not declare it, because concealing it is part of his scheming and beautifying. It may also be the lam of consequence and outcome, like His words ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become an enemy to them and a source of grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Because he did not call them to the Blaze; rather it happened that their affair, from his calling, became that."

Al-sa'ir is the intense fire, and it became predominant in the language of the Shari'ah as a designation for Jahannam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 7:

﴿Those who disbelieve, for them is a severe punishment, and those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) which conveys the sense of a summary conclusion (fadhlaka) and inference drawn from what has preceded.

This resumption points to the fact that those who disbelieve are the party of Satan (hizb al-Shaytan), because when He mentioned that his party are among the companions of the Blaze (as-sa'ir), and here judged that those who disbelieve have a severe punishment, it is known that those who disbelieve are among the companions of the Blaze, since that is the severe punishment. Thus it is known that they are the party of Satan by way of an implicit analogical reasoning (qiyas maṭwiyy). So those who disbelieve are the party of Satan, through their persistence in following him, even if they do not openly declare it, due to their conviction that they constantly abide by what he dictates to them.

Page 263
As for the believing sinners, they are not of his party, because they know his guile, but they follow some of his whisperings driven by desires; yet they nonetheless curse him and disavow him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said during the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed, Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this land of yours, but he has become content with you in matters other than that, which you consider trivial among your deeds."

The mention of "those who believe and do righteous deeds" is a completion, indicating that those who were not of his party have attained good things.

The verse has indicated two extremes of misguidance and guidance, and has passed over what lies between them of degrees, so that it is known that whatever lies between them obtains its share, according to which of the two groups their conditions most resemble. This is in keeping with the Qur'an's manner of placing the believer between fear and hope, and between expectation and awe.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 8:**

﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good, [equal to one who is guided]? Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So do not let your soul expire in regret over them. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾

When the warning to people against the deception of Satan (al-Shaytan) was given, and when they were awakened to his enmity toward mankind, and when people were divided into two groups, one group that was deceived by Satan's schemes and was misled by his delusion and did not oppose him, and another group that took precaution against him, guarded against his plotting, and avoided walking his paths, and then (people were divided) into a disbeliever who will be punished and a believer who is righteous and blessed, this was followed by an allusion to the deserved punishment of the Blaze (al-Sa'ir) for the party of Satan. It was also followed by consoling the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding those among the community of his call who had not escaped the snares of Satan, with a gentle manner of consolation. So He branched (this) off from everything that preceded it, with His saying ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good﴾ up to His saying ﴿what they do﴾. Beginning it with the fa' of consequence (fa' al-tafri') links it to what came before, so that the mind returns to what was related of their circumstances. Thus the branching is upon His saying ﴿He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir: 6]. Then (it is further marked by) presenting the branched statement in the form of a denying interrogative, and by bringing in the relative pronoun whose complement hints at the cause of the intended predicate. Thus it is indicated that their being in this state arises from Satan's making their evil deeds attractive to them. The one who makes evil deeds attractive is Satan, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Satan made their deeds attractive to them﴾ [al-Naml: 24]. So they saw their evil deeds as good, and they clung to them, and they did not accept the advice of any adviser or the message of any messenger.

[p. 264]

The word "man" (من) here is a relative pronoun referring to a group of people, as indicated by His saying at the end of the statement, ﴿so do not let your soul expire in regret over them﴾. Indeed, the branching of this upon His saying ﴿He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir: 6] also indicates it. The "man" is in the position of the nominative of the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted for brevity, since what precedes it indicates it. That predicate is His saying ﴿For those who disbelieve there is a severe punishment﴾ [Fatir: 7], following His saying ﴿He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir: 6]. Its estimate, with respect to what the party of Satan deserves of punishment, is: "Is it you who guides the one whose deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good? Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills."

Its estimate, with respect to the Prophet (ﷺ), is: "Let not his destiny grieve you, for indeed Allah is aware of him."

Branched from this is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾, and branched from this is His saying ﴿So do not let your soul expire in regret over them﴾. That is: "So do not do that," meaning: "It is not fitting for you to do that, for they brought themselves into that state by Satan's making (their deeds) attractive to them and their seeing that as good, and this is from their own actions. So why would you grieve over them?"

This statement is one that is indicated by the antithesis in His saying ﴿For those who disbelieve there is a severe punishment, and for those who believe and do righteous deeds there is forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [Fatir: 7]. This indicates that disbelief is evil and that faith is good. Thus the one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him is the disbeliever, and its opposite is the believer. A parallel to this construction is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Is one upon whom the word of punishment has been justified [to be equal to one who is saved]? Can you then save those who are in the Fire?﴾ [al-Zumar: 19], in Surat al-Zumar. It was also discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Is He who is standing over every soul in what it has earned [like those who associate partners with Him]?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], in Surat al-Ra'd.

Tazyin (embellishment, making attractive) is making appear good that which is not good, in part or in whole. Here the opposite of it is explicitly mentioned in His saying "the evil of his deed," meaning: their evil deeds were presented to them in a good form so that they would proceed toward them eagerly. This was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Naml.

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ is a branched clause, and it is an affirmation for consolation and a despairing (of guidance) for one whom Allah has not created the causes of guidance toward the truth in, from sound reflection and fair disputation.

[p. 265]

The attribution of misguidance and guidance to Allah is through the fact that He is the Creator of the causes of misguidance and guidance. This is from His exalted disposition through creation. It is a profound secret of wisdom whose depth cannot be grasped, and it has principles and rules which I will explain, God willing, in the treatise on qada' and qadar (divine decree and predestination).

His saying ﴿So do not let your soul expire in regret over them﴾ is a clause branched from the branched clause ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him...﴾, and it is thus interpreted as branching from the two clauses, so that the construction is interpreted to be: "Will you then grieve over those whose evil deeds were made attractive to them, so that they saw them as good and chose for themselves the path of error? Indeed, Allah has led them astray by their own choice, and He has acted by His will. So it is He who led them astray and guided others by His will and His desire, by which He willed the existence of beings, not by His command and His pleasure, with which He called people to right guidance." ﴿So do not let your soul expire in regret over them﴾: their regret is only over themselves, since they were content with following Satan and rejected following the guidance of Allah, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾, recording against them that they brought ruin upon themselves by their own doing in what they fell into.

So Allah guided them by sending His Messenger that he might lead them to what pleases Him, and Allah led them astray by creating their souls averse to guidance, through a chain of countless beings that none encompasses except His knowledge, and all of which are manifestations of His wisdom. Had He willed, He would have made the chains of existence in an order other than this, and He would have guided all people; and each of them is made easy by His facilitation toward what He knows of them. So the familiar arrangement was departed from in favor of this wondrous arrangement. It is expressed with a denying interrogative and a prohibition that affirms (the matter). A parallel to this verse in this style is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Is one upon whom the word of punishment has been justified...? Can you then save those who are in the Fire?﴾ [al-Zumar: 19] in Surat al-Zumar. The original structure of its wording is: "Is one upon whom the word of punishment has been justified—you save him from the Fire? Can you then save those who are in the Fire?" However, this verse has been enriched by the parenthetical insertion, and its final branching in it is a prohibition, while the other is stripped of the parenthetical insertion, and its final branching in it is a denying interrogative.

The prohibition is directed at the very self of the Messenger (ﷺ): that his soul should not expire in regret over the astray. It was not addressed to him by saying "So do not let (yourself) expire over them in regret." The Messenger (ﷺ) and his self are identical.

[p. 266]

So directing the prohibition at his self rather than saying "so do not expire over them in regret" is to indicate that the "going away" (dhahab) is metaphorically used for perishing and annihilation, as one says: "Her soul flew away like a spark," and similar expressions in their speech are numerous, such as the saying of the Bedouin poet among the poets of the Hamasah:

I say to the soul, in sorrow and consolation,
"One of my two hands has struck me, and it did not intend it."

The purpose is that the distribution of the prohibition and the address over two things, in outward appearance, achieves a benefit, for it is a repetition of the address and the prohibition for both of them. This is the method called al-tajrid (abstraction), counted among the embellishments, and the benefit of this repetition is to firm up the sentence in the soul. Something close to this was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And they deceive none but themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-hasrah (regret) was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be decided﴾ [Maryam: 39] in Surat Maryam.

The word "hasarat" (regrets) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning: "Do not destroy yourself for the sake of regret over them." It is like His saying ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3], and His saying ﴿And his eyes became white from the grief﴾ [Yusuf: 84], meaning: from the grief of his soul, not from the grief of the two eyes.

The plural "hasarat" is used even though the noun of genus is capable of indicating the recurrence of instances. This is intended to draw attention to the intention of many instances of the kind of regret, because the destruction of the soul occurs when regrets succeed one another, since the one regretted remains lasting. So each regret leaves a sore and grief in the soul until it reaches the limit that the soul cannot bear, and the heart is ruptured by it. It is known in medicine that death from intense pain, like severe beating and the cutting of limbs, is caused by the disruption of the heart's motion from the successive arrival of pains upon it.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited ﴿So do not let your soul...﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', and a raf' (nominative) on "nafsuka" (your soul), as a prohibition addressed to his soul, which is a clear metonymy for his prohibition. Abu Ja'far recited it with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', and a nasb (accusative) on "nafsaka" (your soul), as a prohibition to the Messenger that he should not cause his soul to perish.

This verse contains four fa's, all of which indicate causation and branching, and it is by them that the wording of the verse reaches this extreme concision that borders on inimitability (i'jaz). In their combination there is the rhetorical embellishment of gathering similar elements (husn jam' al-naza'ir).

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ is suitable for conveying patience and forbearance, meaning: Indeed Allah is

[p. 267]

Knowing of their doing in opposing His command. So just as He, out of His forbearance, did not hasten to seize them, so you should take Allah as your model and adorn yourself with those of His attributes that you are able to bear. Within this is a metonymy for their not escaping punishment for their evil deeds. There is no meaning in this clause of giving the reason for ﴿So do not let your soul expire in regret over them﴾, because the distress of the soul of the Messenger (ﷺ) was not for the sake of delaying their punishment, but for the sake of their not being guided.

The emphasis of the predicate with "inna" (indeed) is either a representation of the state of the Messenger (ﷺ) by the state of one whom the regret over them has distracted from reflecting on Allah's granting them respite; so the predicate is emphasized for him with ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾; or it is to make the emphasis merely a matter of attention to the predicate, so that "inna" serves the function of the fa' of consequence, and the clause becomes purely for affirming consolation and an implicit allusion to requital.

He expressed it with "yasna'un" (they do/make) rather than "ya'maluna" (they work/do), to indicate that they devise schemes against the Prophet (ﷺ) and against the Muslims. So this statement serves as a notification of the existence of another motive for turning away from regret over them. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the intended referent is Abu Jahl and his party.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 9:**

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus will be the resurrection.﴾

Since the argument at the beginning of the surah was made by means of the fact that Allah originated the heavens and the earth and those in the heavens who inhabit them, which is the greatest proof of His singularity in divinity, He here repeats the argument through the variation of conditions between the heaven and the earth. This takes the form of sending the winds, forming the clouds, and sending down rain. This is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon His words ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1].

The Name of Majesty (Allah) is made explicit in a place where a pronoun could have been used, instead of saying "And He is the One who sent the winds." This is so that the pronoun refers back to the name of Allah in His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ [Fatir: 8].

From among the proofs of oneness, the one chosen is the indication of the gathering of the causes of rain, so that from this there may be an arrival at the parallel of the revival of the dead after states of annihilation, through the effects of this marvelous work. And [the point is] that He who created the means of reviving the earth is able to create the means of reviving those whom the earth has taken in. This is by way of incorporation (idmaj).

Page 268

Since the purpose of the argument is the occurrence of revival and the establishment of its occurrence, the past tense is used in His word "sent" (arsala). As for changing it to the present tense in His word ﴿so they stir up clouds﴾ (fa-tuthir), this is to narrate the marvelous state in which the stirring of clouds by the winds takes place. This is a method of eloquent speakers regarding an act whose particularity involves a condition that is strange and engages the listener. It is similar to the saying of Ta'abbata Sharran:

*That I have met the ghoul, as she swoops down in a wasteland, like a page, a level expanse,*
*So I struck her without dismay, and she fell, prostrate upon her hands and her flank.*

He began with "I met" (laqītu) to convey that the event occurred, then followed with "I struck her" (adribuhā) to evoke that marvelous image of his boldness and steadfastness, so much so that it is as if they were seeing him in that state. The verb of sending was not put in the present tense in this verse, unlike His words in Surat al-Rum "Allah is the One who sends the winds" and so on, because the aim here is an argument from what is actually occurring, in order to show the possibility of its like. As for the verse of Surat al-Rum, the aim there is an argument for the renewal of Allah's work and His blessings.

The discussion concerning the winds and clouds has preceded more than once, the first of which was in Surat al-Baqarah.

In His words ﴿We drive them﴾ (fa-saqnāhu), after His words ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾, there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person absent to the first person speaking.

His words ﴿Thus will be the resurrection﴾ follow the same path as His words ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true﴾ [Fatir: 5] and the verses after it, in affirming the resurrection together with the confirmation of the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he reported about it. However, what came before it was taken from the implication of the indication (fahwa al-dalala), when it appeared in the proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what he reported of monotheism. It was taken by way of the indication of approximation (dalalat al-taqrib) to the occurrence of the resurrection, since their intellects had been brought to acknowledge the possibility of return after annihilation, so that from the flash of the Messenger's (ﷺ) truthfulness and the flash of possibility there arises what guides their minds to the soundness of affirming the occurrence of the resurrection.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿Thus will be the resurrection﴾ refers to what was mentioned in His words ﴿and give life thereby to the earth﴾. The more apparent view is that the demonstrative refers to the whole pictured condition, meaning: like that perfectly arranged, precisely executed work, We will perform a work by which there will be the resurrection, by Allah preparing celestial and terrestrial events, or a combination of them, until, when their effects are aligned and bodies become fit to receive their souls, Allah commands the first and second blasts, and then the bodies are standing and looking on. This is the parallel of Allah's command to breathe souls into embryos when their preparation to receive souls is complete.

Page 269

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) a approximation of this in a similar manner, as reported by Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shaybah, and something close to it in Sahih Muslim, from ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It was said to the Messenger of Allah: How does Allah give life to the dead, and what is the sign of that in His creation? He said: Have you passed by a valley that was barren, then you passed by it while it was quivering green?" It was said: "Yes." He said: "So thus does Allah give life to the dead, and that is His sign in His creation." In some narrations from Ibn Razin al-ʿUqayli, the questioner is Razin.

The majority read "the winds" (al-riyāḥ) in the plural form. Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i read "the wind" (al-rīḥ) in the singular. The definite article indicating the genus (lam al-jins) applies equally to the singular and the plural.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 10 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Whoever desires honour—to Allah belongs all honour.﴾ Earlier, two kinds of delusion were mentioned in summary in His words: ﴿So let not the worldly life delude you, and let not the Deluder deceive you concerning Allah﴾ [Fatir: 5]. He then went on to detail the second delusion, from His words: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾ [Fatir: 6], and what follows from it of warning about the snares of his plotting, the outbreak of the poison of his deceit, caution against the fatal consequences of following him, and showing the difference between those who fall into his traps and those who are safe from his afflictions. This was to hasten the detailing of what is more important and fundamental, and he left the detailing of the first delusion until here.

Since the greatest delusion of the polytheists in their polytheism arose from accepting the teachings of their great men and chiefs, and since the greatest motive of the leaders in misleading their common folk and their clients was what they found of honour and of being captivated by love of leadership—for the leaders bring honour to themselves, and the followers take pride in the strength of their leaders—therefore the desire for honour was the basis of the polytheists' solidarity with one another and their united opposition to Islam. So the address was directed to them to expose their being deceived by their pursuit of honour in this world. Every person who holds fast to the cord of polytheism, turning away from reflecting on the call of Islam, is held by nothing but the desire for honour. Therefore the Qur'an calls out to them that whoever has this as his obstacle from the true religion should know that the true honour lies in following Islam, and that the honour they have is as nothing.

"Man" (مَن) is conditional, and its answer is ﴿then to Allah belongs all honour﴾. The establishment of honour for Allah is not ordered in existence upon the occurrence of this condition, so it is determined that what comes after the particle of the apodosis (the fa') is the reason for the answer. It has been placed in its stead and dispensed with by it for brevity, and so that deriving it from within the discourse fixes it in the mind of the listener. The estimate is: whoever desires honour, let him respond to the call of Islam, for in it is honour, because all honour belongs to Allah the Exalted. As for the honour to which they cling, it is like the spider's thread, for it is frail and decayed. This is a method commonly used in a context where the aim is to alert the addressee to an error in his assumption, as in the words of al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad al-'Absi concerning the killing of Malik ibn Zuhayr al-'Absi:

Whoever is delighted by the killing of Malik, let him come to our women at the start of day;
he will find the women bareheaded, lamenting him by night before the dawn breaks.

He meant: whoever is pleased by the killing of Malik, let him not enjoy his pleasure nor suppose he has attained his aim, for if he comes to the court of our women, his joy will turn into grief and sorrow, as he finds clear signs of vengeance being taken on his killer, since the custom is that the slain is not lamented by women except when his blood has been avenged. This is what al-Marzuqi explained, and it is what I received from our shaykh al-Wazir. There is another explanation of the two verses.

It may also be the reverse, which is confirming the addressee in his knowledge, as in His words: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah, then indeed the term of Allah is coming﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 5].

Close to this usage is what is intended to show the difference between one who is characterised by the content of the condition and one who is characterised by the content of the answer, as in the words of al-Nabigha:

Whoever has already fulfilled his need from a friend—then indeed I have not fulfilled my needs from you.

And the words of Dabi ibn al-Harith:

Whoever has made his dwelling in Medina at nightfall—then indeed I and Qayyar in it are strangers.

And the words of al-Kilabi:

Whoever is spoken to will turn away—then indeed I and my she-camel are two who turn away, at Hajr, toward the people of the protected pasture.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase here conveys restriction, and it is a claimed (ideational) restriction, because the slight honour the polytheists have is not taken into account. That is: honour belongs to Allah, not to them.

Among its uses is that the answer follows the condition in actual occurrence, which is the original use, as in His words: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty life, We hasten for him therein what We will﴾ [al-Isra': 18], and His words: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾ [Hud: 15].

"Jami'an" (all) conveys comprehensiveness, so it serves as an emphasis for the claimed restriction. Thus three emphases are obtained: the restriction counts as two emphases, and "jami'an" counts as one emphasis. This is close to His words: ﴿Do they seek honour with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139], for in it there are two emphases: emphasis by "inna" and emphasis by "jami'an". That verse was revealed at a time of the strength of Islam, so no added emphasis was needed there. The discussion of "jami'an" has already preceded at His words: ﴿and the Day He gathers them all﴾ in Surat Saba'.

"Jami'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-'izzah" (honour), and it is as if it were an adjective of the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul: honour in its entirety belongs to Allah, none of it deviating so as to be established for another, because the honour customarily known among people is as nothing, since its possessor is never free of need and weakness, whereas true honour belongs to Allah.

The definiteness of "al-'izzah" is the definiteness of the genus. "Al-'izzah" means nobility and protection from being touched by harm. The meaning is: whoever desires honour but turns away from the call of Allah, out of holding on to what he imagines for himself of honour, is mistaken, for he has no honour; he is like one who spills water for the glitter of a mirage. True honour belongs to Allah, who called them through His Messenger. The honour of the Master is shared by His party and His allies in some portion; so if they followed the command of Allah and joined His party, the honour of Allah would become theirs, and that is the lasting honour. For the honour of the polytheists is followed by the humiliation of defeat, slaughter and capture in this world, and the humiliation of disgrace and punishment in the Hereafter, whereas the honour of the believers increases in this world and has degrees of perfection in the Hereafter.

﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾

Just as He followed the detailing of Satan's deception with its consequences in the Hereafter, with His words ﴿He only invites his party to be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir: 6] and onward, and with mention of the opposite of its consequences from the condition of the believers, so likewise He followed the detailing of the deception of the self with its consequences for its people, and with mention of its opposite as well, so that the outcomes of the two deceptions and their opposites meet in one meeting-place. But in the first case the consequence of the people of deception by Satan was mentioned first, then the consequence of their opposites was mentioned; here the order is reversed, because the mention of Allah's honour has preceded, so what is appropriate to the effects of Allah's honour upon His party and soldiers is put first.

The sentence ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ is resumptive, a fresh beginning, occasioned by the detailing of the deception into which one falls.

The intended meaning is that the deeds of the believers are what benefit, so that people may know that the deeds of the polytheists are a vain striving. All acts of drawing near (to Allah) return to words and deeds. Words are those which are praise of Allah the Exalted, seeking forgiveness, supplication, and calling people to righteous deeds; their mention has preceded at His words: ﴿And speak a correct word﴾ [al-Ahzab: 70] in Surat al-Ahzab. Deeds contain many acts of drawing near. The polytheists used to draw near to their idols by praise and glorification, as Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "Exalt Hubal!" They also sought to draw near through acts of circumambulation, pilgrimage, and aiding the distressed; but all of this was mixed with association, because they intended by them drawing near to the gods. For this reason they set up idols in the Ka'bah, placed Hubal, their greatest, on the roof of the Ka'bah, and placed Isaf and Na'ilah above al-Safa and al-Marwah, so that their rites to Allah would be mixed with the worship of the gods, realizing the meaning of association in all their deeds.

When the prepositional phrase in His words ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ was fronted, it conveyed that every good word offered to other than Allah is of no avail.

As for His words ﴿and righteous deed raises it﴾: "deed" is the counterpart of "word," meaning the actions that are not speech. The pronoun of raising refers back to the pronoun in the prepositional phrase "to Him," whose referent is the name of Allah in His words ﴿then to Allah belongs all honour﴾; and the object pronoun in "yarfa'uhu" refers to "righteous deed," meaning Allah raises the righteous deed.

"Su'ud" (ascent) means going up to a high place. "Raf'" (raising) means moving a thing from a place to a place higher than it. Thus "su'ud" is used metaphorically for attaining great rank, and it is a metonymy for acceptance in His presence.

"Raf'" in its literal sense is moving a body from its place to a higher place; here it is a metonymy for acceptance by a great One, because the imagination conceives the great as being at an exalted place. So each of "yas'adu" and "yarfa'u" is a subsidiary of an implicit metaphor (makniyyah), in that the aspect of acceptance by Allah the Exalted is likened to an elevated place that only what ascends to it can reach.

So His words "the deed" are the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "yarfa'uhu." The verbal predicate built upon the nominal subject conveys that the subject is restricted to the predicate; and when there is joined to this the context of the sentence following the context of the restrictive sentence, which implies that the restriction applies to it through the context, since the situation is unified (for it is not conceivable that the ascent of the good word would be restricted to the divine side, and then another be given a share with Him in raising the righteous deed), the meaning of restriction is established. So the meaning becomes: Allah is the One who accepts from the believers their words and their righteous deeds.

The deed of righteousness is given a predicate in the form of a nominal sentence "yarfa'uhu" and not coordinated with "al-kalim al-tayyib" in the rule of ascent to Allah, although the two predicates are equal, for two benefits: the first is an indication that the type of righteous deed is more important than the type of good word in general, since most righteous deeds are broader in benefit than most good words—except the two testimonies and what has been reported as excellent among words in the Sunnah, such as the supplication of the Day of 'Arafah. Therefore the raising of it is attributed to Allah Himself, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever gives a charity from lawful earnings—and Allah accepts only what is good—the All-Merciful receives it in His right hand, and both His hands are right, and He nurtures it for him as one of you nurtures his foal, until it becomes like a mountain."

The second: the good word takes on form in the air, so attributing ascent to it suits its nature. As for the righteous deed, it is accidental states of acting and acted-upon entities, so attributing ascent to it is not fitting; rather it is appropriate that it be made the object of a raising that falls upon it and lifts it upward.
