﴿As for those who plot evil deeds, for them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those—it will perish﴾

This is a group among those who desire honour from the polytheists, namely those whom Allah mentioned in His words: ﴿And when those who disbelieve plotted against you to confine you, or kill you, or expel you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] and so on. Abu al-'Aliyah said this. Their coordination with ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾ is a singling-out of them by mention, because of what they were distinguished by in devising plots. It is coordination of the particular upon the general, for the sake of giving attention to its mention.

Plotting (makr) is devising to inflict harm upon another secretly, lest he take his precaution, and its verb is intransitive. It is connected to the one harmed through the preposition "bi," which indicates accompaniment; one says "makara bi-fulan" (he plotted against so-and-so). And it is connected to the means of the plot through the causal "bi," as one says "makara bi-fulan bi-qatlihi" (he plotted against so-and-so by killing him). The accusative of "al-sayyi'at" here is because it is an adjective of the verbal noun of the plot, standing in the place of an absolute object specifying the kind of the act; so it is as if it were said: "those who plot the evil plot." It should have been that the adjective of the verbal noun be singular, as in His words: ﴿and the evil plot does not encompass except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. But since what is intended here is to alert that the allies of Satan have various kinds of plotting, the expression was shifted from the singular to the plural, and it was put in the feminine plural form to indicate the meaning of the acts of plotting, so that each one of their plots is an evil deed, just as this occurs in the word (salihah) in the verse of Jarir:

"How can I be hurt, when there are ever good (ṣāliḥah) ones from the family of La'm in the unseen, coming to me?"

Meaning: many wrongful acts. The kinds of their schemes are what is mentioned in His saying, ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to restrain you or kill you or expel you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30].

The definite article in "al-sayyi'at" (the evil deeds) is the definite article of genus (al-ta'rif al-jins). The relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) is used to indicate that the content of the relative clause is the cause of the ruling that follows it, meaning: "for them is a severe punishment in recompense for their scheming." The verb is in the present tense (al-mudari') in the relative clause to indicate that their scheming is renewed and continuous, and that it is their habit and their constant practice.

When Allah threatened them with a severe punishment for their scheming, He informed them that their scheming would not prosper or find a market, and that Allah would nullify it, so they would gain nothing from it in this world, and would be harmed by it in the Hereafter. So He said, ﴿And the scheming of those—it will perish﴾.

Page 275

They are referred to by the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) rather than by the pronoun that the apparent context would require, in order to distinguish them most completely. Thus this alludes to the clear distinction of the scheming attributed to them and its manifestness in the knowledge of Allah and the knowledge of His Messenger ﷺ, through what Allah had informed him of it. It is as though they and their scheming were pointed to with a single demonstrative, by way of brevity.

The pronoun (damir) placed between "the scheming of those" and "will perish" is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), since no other reading is possible. Similar to it is His saying, ﴿Did they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104].

The most preferred of the grammarians' opinions is that of al-Mazini (al-Mazini: a grammarian of the Basran school), that the separating pronoun is followed by the present-tense verb, and his proof is His saying, ﴿And the scheming of those—it will perish﴾, with a present-tense verb and not another form. Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani agreed with him in his commentary on Abu 'Ali al-Farisi's al-Idah. Abu Hayyan disagreed with both of them and said: "No one, as far as we know, has held this view." I say: The reason the present-tense verb occurs after the separating pronoun is that the present tense indicates renewal. When the context requires conveying the renewal of the occurrence of the act together with the affirmation and permanence of the judgmental attribution, the eloquent speaker has no way to combine the two aims except by using the separating pronoun, to convey permanence and emphasis, since this cannot be conveyed by a nominal sentence. This was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿And those are the successful﴾. So the separating pronoun here conveys restriction (al-qasr), meaning: their scheming perishes and not anything else. It is known that "anything else" here implies an allusion that Allah schemes against them with a scheme that strikes them at their most vulnerable point, in accordance with His saying, ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54].

The root meaning of al-bawar is the slump of trade and the failure of goods to sell. It is used here figuratively for the frustration of an action, based on the resemblance between what they plotted of scheming, with their eagerness to harm the Prophet ﷺ, and what a merchant arranges, takes out of his bags, and lays out on his shelves in the middle of his merchandise-laden caravan in order to attract the eagerness of buyers. Then none of the people of the market turns to it, and so he returns from his caravan with empty hands and an empty bag, having gained nothing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 11:

﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then He made you into pairs.﴾ This is a return to presenting the proofs of God's Oneness, by evidence drawn from human beings themselves, after He had first presented to them what comes from the evidence of the horizons, in His words ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾ [Fatir: 9]. This is like His words:

Page 276
﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ [Fussilat: 53], and His words ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]. So He began by reminding them of the first origin of creation, from dust, which is a matter known to all mankind: that their origin, the first human being, was created from clay. This became an established truth in human knowledge, and it is what logic calls "premises accepted as standing in place of things perceived by the senses."

Then He led them on to the second creation through the evidence of the creation of offspring from a drop of semen, a knowledge firmly settled in souls. This comes by witnessing the present and analogizing the absent to the witnessed: just as a person is certain that his offspring was created from his own semen, he is certain that he himself was created from the semen of his parents, and so on upward until one reaches the creation of the children of Adam and Eve.

The word nutfah (drop) was discussed earlier, at His words ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen?﴾ [al-Kahf: 37], in Surat al-Kahf.

His words ﴿then He made you into pairs﴾ point to a state within the second creation, which is its condition of pairing. The "then" (thumma) here is a conjunction of sentences, and it indicates a ranked sequence, which is more important for the purpose, namely the demonstration of the Creator's wondrous craftsmanship, glorified is He. This is distributed over the meaning of His words "then from a drop of semen."

The meaning is: then from a drop of semen, and He has made you pairs for the composition of that drop. Thus, reasoning from the precision of the making of the human species is among the greatest proofs of the Maker's oneness. And in it there is sufficiency, so that one need not reflect on the craftsmanship of the rest of the animals.

Al-azwaj (pairs) is the plural of zawj, which is that which becomes a pair (zawj) by the joining of a single individual to it, that is, an even partner. Its application has become widespread to the male class together with the female class, because each male individual of any class needs a female of his own class, and vice versa.

﴿No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾
After the reasoning from what is at the beginning of the second creation, namely the mingling of the two drops, comes reasoning from what arises from that by way of the stages that befall the drop in the womb, which are the stages of pregnancy from its beginning until delivery.

Page 277
Included in this is an indication that draws attention to the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah over hidden and manifest beings. And because knowledge of hidden things is of higher rank, mention of conception is placed before mention of birth. The purpose of conjoining birth is to prevent the supposition that knowledge stops at hidden things, which belong to the unseen, and not at manifest things, by one's being preoccupied with managing their hidden aspects, as is the custom of great scholars among people. It also shows the impossibility of directing the will of creation toward something unknown to the one who wills it.

The exception is an exceptive clause emptied from the generality of states. The bi (with) denotes accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Nor is a long-lived person granted length of life, nor is anything taken from his life, except that it is in a Book. Indeed that is easy for Allah﴾
Certainly, speech about creation entails mention of death, which is decreed upon every human being. So He mentioned His knowledge of the appointed terms and lifespans, to draw attention to the vastness of divine knowledge.

Ta'mir (granting long life) means making a person long-lived, that is, remaining alive. For 'umr is the duration of life; one says: 'amira fulan, like fariha, nasara and daraba, when he remained for a time. So the meaning of 'ammarahu, with doubling, is: He made him remain for a period beyond the period customary in the lifespans of the generations. For this reason it is contrasted with the reduction of life, and for this reason the one who is granted long life is described only with the passive form, so one says: 'ummira fulan, and he is mu'ammar (long-lived). In these generations it has prevailed that death occurs between sixty and seventy, and what lies between them; this is the customary lifespan. The one who is long-lived is one whose life exceeds seventy, and the one whose life is reduced is one who dies before sixty. For this reason the most preferred opinion regarding granting long life to a missing person (mafqud) among the jurists of the Maliki school is to take him as reaching seventy years from the date of his birth. The judiciary in Tunisia ruled that he is not considered beyond eighty years. They said: because those who live to eighty are not few, so it is not proper to rule that the missing person is dead until after that, because inheritance depends on it, and there is no inheritance on the basis of doubt; and because after ruling him dead his wife is married, and a condition for the validity of marriage is that the woman be free of a marital bond, and the condition cannot be applied when there is doubt about it. This is an inference that is open to question.

The pronoun in "min 'umrihi" (from his life) refers back to mu'ammar (long-lived one) by interpreting mu'ammar as (a person), as if it were said: "nor is anyone granted length of life, nor is the life of anyone reduced," that is, the life of one person or another. This is speech that proceeds with tolerance in such usage, relying on the hearers understanding the intended meaning, as in His words ﴿And if a man leaves an inheritance as kalalah, or a woman, and he has a brother or a sister, then each of the two shall have a sixth...﴾ [al-Nisa': 12], because it is evident that the dead person does not become an heir to one who has already inherited from him, nor does an heir become a deceased person inherited by his own heir.

The Book is a metaphor for the knowledge of Allah, which nothing known escapes, just as a written thing is not added to or subtracted from. It is also possible that Allah makes existing things, like books, in which the terms are inscribed in detail, and that is easy among the creatures of Allah, the Exalted. For this reason He said:

﴿Indeed that is easy for Allah﴾, that is, this recording does not impose any difficulty or burden upon Him.

Here arises the general problem that results from the apparent conflict between the proofs that everything proceeds according to what has already been foreordained in the knowledge of Allah from eternity, and the attribution of things to causes, and the seeking of what is desired through those causes and the avoidance of what is disliked. How, then, can increase and decrease in lifespans be established in this verse, while they are in a Book and in a knowledge that does not admit change? And how is one encouraged, for instance, by the statement that charity increases life, and that maintaining family ties prolongs life?

The resolution of this and similar matters is the fundamental principle distinguishing between a thing being known to Allah, the Exalted, and a thing being willed. For knowledge relates to things that exist and things that do not exist, while will relates to bringing things into existence in accordance with the knowledge that they will come to be. So people are addressed to strive for what the will relates to. When the will relates to a thing, we know that Allah knew its occurrence. The conduct and endeavors of people are only signs of what Allah knew for them. Thus the charity of the giver is a sign that Allah knew his long life, and Allah, the Exalted, manifests His known things in forms of honor or humiliation, so that the order upon which Allah founded this world may be completed, and everything He willed from this creation may harmonize in ways in which some parts do not disrupt others, and all of that is required by lofty wisdom. There is no resolution of this problem except this answer, and everything else, though it may convince at first, ultimately leads back to where the problem began.

[Page 279]

﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant for drinking, and that one is salt, bitter. And from each you eat fresh flesh, and you extract ornaments which you wear, and you see the ships plowing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

This is a transition from reasoning based on the conditions of the atmospheric regions between heaven and earth, which establish God Most High's sole divinity, to reasoning based on what lies on the earth of seas and rivers, and on the additional indication in their attributes beyond the indication of the existence of their substances, concerning the greatness of God Most High's creation. This argument is formulated in a wonderful style, in that it is limited to drawing attention to the divine wisdom in creatures, namely the law of their differentiation through various properties and the unity of their kinds in similar properties, as evidence for the precise craftsmanship of God Most High, like His saying: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [13:4]. This includes the argument from the creation of the two seas themselves, because mentioning the difference in their taste necessarily implies remembering their creation.

The estimate is: "And He created the two seas, the sweet and the salt, in one form, and varied their accidents." There is therefore an elliptical concision (ijaz hadhf, concision by omission) in the speech. The difference between the two seas in taste was put forward from this discourse and was limited to it, because it is the intended point of the argument through the varied kinds of evidence for the precise craftsmanship of God Most High.

In al-Kashshaf: "He struck the two seas, the sweet and the salty, as a parable for the believer and the disbeliever. Then he said, by way of digression (istitrad) in describing the two seas and what is attached to them of His blessing and bounty: ﴿And from each you eat fresh flesh﴾."

In the speech of the Arabs, "sea" (bahr) is the name for abundant water that is still and spread out. The Euphrates and the Tigris are two sweet seas, and the Persian Gulf is salt. The mention of the two seas was previously made at His saying: ﴿And it is He who released the two seas﴾ [25:53], in Surat al-Furqan. They are united in bringing forth fish and ornaments, namely pearls and coral. The best of these is found in the Persian Gulf, where the two rivers empty, and the sweet water of the two rivers mixed with the salt water of the sea has an effect on the quality of the pearl, as we explained previously in Surat al-Nahl. So His saying ﴿And from each you eat fresh flesh﴾ is universal (kulliyyah), while His saying ﴿and you extract ornaments﴾ is collective (kull), not universal, because from their totality you extract ornaments. The word "kull" is suitable for both meanings, so the conjunction of "and you extract" is a use of the homonym in both its meanings.

[Page 280]

The difference between the two seas in sweetness and saltness is evidence of God's precise craftsmanship. The divergence in some of what is extracted from them, and the similarity in some of it, is another evidence of precise craftsmanship, and this is among the varied forms of argument.

Al-'adhb (sweet) is the sweet, with a pleasant sweetness to the taste.

Al-milh (with a kasra on the mim) is the thing described as salty by its very nature, not by having salt put into it. As for a thing into which salt is put until it acquires saltness, it is called mali<u>h</u> (salted), and it is not called milh.

The meaning of ﴿pleasant for drinking﴾ is that its drinking does not burden the soul with aversion. It is derived from al-isagha, which is the ability to swallow a drink without choking or disgust. 'Abdullah ibn Ya'rub said:

"So drink became pleasant to me, though before I was nearly choking on scalding water."

Al-ujaj is the very salty. The word "sea" was mentioned at His saying ﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea﴾ [6:59], in Surat al-An'am, and the rest of the verse has a parallel previously in the beginning of Surat al-Nahl.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿in it ships plowing﴾ is the reverse of the verse in Surat al-Nahl, because this verse is directed as an argument for the precise craftsmanship of God Most High in creatures, and the favour is embedded within it by His saying "you eat."

﴿And you extract ornaments﴾ and His saying ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾: the primary aim of their context is the argument for the great craftsmanship, and so it is the most important here. Since the floating of ships on the water, so that they do not sink, is more manifest in the argument for great craftsmanship than what is mentioned of blessing and favour, what indicates it was put forward, namely the adverbial sense of being in the sea. The plowing in the sea is also a sign of God's craftsmanship, through creating the means of that and inspiring it, but the danger of travel arising from that description, or what comes to mind, was delayed here, because it is a consequence of the purpose and not its aim. It entails the blessing of facilitating journeys to cover distances which, if covered by caravans, would prolong the durations of travel.

From here there flashes the glimmer of the difference between this verse and the verse of Surat al-Nahl, in that the verb "that you may seek" (li-tabtaghu) is not conjoined with the conjunction "and" here, whereas its counterpart in the verse of al-Nahl is conjoined, because seeking is here attached to "plowing" as a stopping upon the purpose of fronting the adverbial phrase. In the verse of al-Nahl, the plowing is mentioned among the favours, because by it journeys are facilitated. Then the phrase "plowing" was separated from its cause by the adverbial phrase "in it," so that what the adverbial phrase indicates became a separation with an embedded purpose (idmaj, embedding), namely the argument for great craftsmanship by the floating of ships on water. When it was intended to move from that to another purpose, namely returning to the favour of plowing for the blessing of commerce in the sea, the different-in-purpose element was conjoined.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verses 13–14:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day, and He causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term.﴾

This is an argument against them, drawing upon the signs in the appearances of the heavens, which demonstrate the wondrous craftsmanship of God in the greatest of created things, so that they may thereby remember that He is the One God.

The discussion of the parallel of this verse has already occurred in Surah Luqman, except that in this verse there is the phrase "﴿each running for a term﴾," where the verb "yajri" (runs) is followed by the preposition "li" (for), whereas in the verse of Surah Luqman the verb "yajri" is followed by the preposition "ila" (to). It was said that "li" may carry the meaning of "ila" in indicating the endpoint (intiha'), so the difference between the two verses is a variation (tafannun) in composition. Al-Zamakhshari rejected this view in Surah Luqman with the strongest rejection, saying: "That is not an interchange of the two particles, and only one of dull nature and narrow mind takes this path. Rather, the two meanings, I mean the endpoint and the exclusivity (ikhtisas), each is suitable for the soundness of the purpose, because your saying 'yajri ila ajal musamma' means that it reaches it, and His saying '﴿yajri li-ajal﴾' means that you intend to attain a term." End of quote. The "li" is taken to mean exclusivity, i.e., it runs for the sake of a term, meaning for its reaching and fulfilment. Endpoint and exclusivity are each suitable to the purpose; that is, the outcome of the two meanings is one, even though the route differs. ﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, while Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾

Since the discussion had been amply furnished with proofs, admonitions, and reminders, which contain enough persuasion for one who sets himself to benefit and be convinced, and since nothing appeared from the condition of these people, despite all this, that would indicate they were turning away from their misguidance, and since this may have produced in the self-important among them a conceit about themselves and a delusion that they were desired to join the community of the Muslims, so that this delusion made them more receptive to the Satan's schemes to adorn for them the idea of clinging to their polytheism, it was fitting that Allah inform them that He is free of need of them, that His religion is not made mighty by people like them, and that He will bring them to annihilation and bring instead a people through whom Islam will be made mighty.

The intended meaning of "O mankind" (ayyuha al-nas) is the polytheists, as is the predominant usage of the Qur'an, and they are the ones addressed by His statement shortly before: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion...﴾ (the verses).

Before the announcement that Allah is free of need of them, an announcement was addressed to them that they are the ones in need of Allah, because that is more effective in humbling their greatness than the awareness that Allah is free of need of them. They are certain that they are in need of Allah, but they are not certain of the implication that follows from their knowledge of this. So the aim is to convey this to them not as an argument, but as a striking of their ears with what they had never been struck with before, in the hope that they might awaken from their heedlessness and withdraw from the delusion of their selves. Moreover, their assembly cannot be free of people of sound intellects capable of reaching the realities of truth. When such people's ears are struck with what they had never heard before, they increase in certainty by witnessing what had been veiled from their insights by the curtains of preoccupation with the temptation of their misguidance, in the hope that whoever Allah has prepared by his nature for faith may believe. As for whoever remains upon his disbelief, his remaining will be mixed with bewilderment, and the taste of life will become bitter to him. So how far is this from what their ears used to receive before, namely their glorification of themselves, their forefathers, and their gods? Do you not see that when they reproached the Prophet (ﷺ) during some of their disputes, they counted against him his insulting of their forefathers? Thus two benefits are achieved by this verse.

The sentence "You are the ones in need" (antum al-fuqara') conveys restriction (qasr) by the definition of both its parts, meaning the restriction of the attribute of need to the people addressed, a restriction relative (qasr idafi) to Allah, that is: you are the ones who are dependent upon Him, and He is not dependent upon you. This is equivalent in meaning to His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾, which implies that they imagine they are angering the Prophet (ﷺ) by not accepting his call. So the proper course is to interpret the restriction derived from the sentence "You are the ones in need" as a relative restriction, which is the restriction of reversal (qasr qalb). As for interpreting it as an absolute restriction and then straining to say that it is claimed ( idda'i), there is no reason for that.

Following the attribute "Self-Sufficient" with "the Praiseworthy" is a completion (takmil). It is a safeguard (ihtiras) to prevent the assumption that, since He is free of need of their obedience and worship, they are excused for not worshipping Him. So it points out that He is described with praise toward whoever worships Him and responds to His call, just as He followed the other verse ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾ with His saying ﴿and if you are grateful, He is pleased with it for you﴾. Among the embellishments (muhassinat) is that "the Praiseworthy" stands in opposition to "to Allah" just as "the Self-Sufficient" stands in opposition to "the ones in need." For since He restricted their need to being directed toward Allah, He restricted Allah's self-sufficiency with the attribute "the Praiseworthy," to convey that His self-sufficiency is accompanied by His generosity, so that He praises whoever turns toward Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verses 16–17:

﴿If He wills, He will remove you and bring a new creation﴾ ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾. This stands in the place of explanation for what the sentence "﴿He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir: 15]" contains, namely the meaning that He is little concerned with their turning away from Islam, and the meaning of His being pleased with those who worship Him. He, exalted is He, is independent of them, and angry with them. If He willed, He would annihilate them and bring other people who would worship Him, so the world would be free of those who disobey the command of Allah. That is within His power, but He gave them respite, out of exercising the attribute of forbearance (ḥilm).

So the will (al-mashi'ah) here is the will that arises from deservingness, meaning that they deserved for Allah to will their destruction, but He gave them respite. It is not the basic will, which is His being free in His action with no one compelling Him, because that does not need to be announced.

It is as though He had removed them from one place to another, because He brings them to the abode of the Hereafter.

The "bringing of a new creation" is used in the sense of bringing into existence people who had not existed and whose existence was not anticipated. That is, He creates a people of mankind who believe in Allah.

Here "creation" (al-khalq) means "the created thing," like His saying, ﴿This is the creation of Allah; so show me what those other than Him have created﴾ [Luqman: 11].

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a near relative.﴾

When the verses before this one were directed toward the purpose of warning, and the address was to mankind, the believers were reassured regarding the consequences of the warning. Thus it was followed by the statement that whoever has not committed a sin will not be struck by the punishment of the bearer of sin in the Hereafter. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous, and leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾. This may be a promise of deliverance from the punishment of this world, since destruction and annihilation befell those who were warned, just as the disbelieving faction was destroyed on the Day of Badr and the faction of believers was saved. Thus this is a specific promise, which is not contradicted by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾, nor by what is related in the hadith of Umm Salamah: "She said, 'O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed while among us are the righteous?' He said, 'Yes, when wickedness becomes abundant.'"

The placement of His saying ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ is like the placement of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whom We willed was saved, and Our punishment is not averted from the criminal people﴾. ﴿You only warn those who fear their Lord unseen, and establish prayer. And whoever purifies himself, he purifies only for himself, and to Allah is the final return﴾. It is a resumptive statement indicating that the Messenger ﷺ felt in himself wonder at the lack of impact of his warning on most of the polytheists, so he was answered that his warning benefits the believers and those who were prepared for faith.

The placing of this verse immediately after the preceding one confirms that the primary aim of the preceding one was admonishing and frightening the polytheists, and conveying the truth to them in order to uproot their claims and delusions concerning resurrection, reckoning and recompense. Allah addressed His Messenger ﷺ so that he would feel that those admonitions were directed to him and that only Muslims benefit from them. It also reinforces the implicit allusion in the first verse to the assurance of the Muslims, by what the generality of warning and threat requires.

The warning is here applied to the attainment of its effect, which is restraint or belief in it, and the intended meaning is not the literal sense of warning, which is informing about the expectation of something disliked, because the context is clearly against the literal meaning, namely the context of the repeated warning to the polytheists from time to time, and that is not far from this verse, for the Prophet ﷺ warned the polytheists throughout the length of his mission. Thus it is determined that the connection of the restricted verb to "those who fear their Lord unseen" is a connection in the sense of the verb's effect being realized.

The purpose of the restriction is that it is a restriction of correction (qasr qalb), because the aim is to alert that the Prophet ﷺ should not suppose that those who do not believe benefit from his warning. Although the form of restriction is suitable for the sense of true restriction, the consideration of the context determines the consideration of a relative restriction (qasr idafi). A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surat (Ya-Sin): ﴿You only warn him who follows the reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾, and His saying: ﴿so remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ in Surat (Qaf), although reminding by the Qur'an encompasses all people.

The unseen (al-ghayb) is what is hidden from you, i.e., those who fear their Lord in their private moments and when they are absent from sight, i.e., those who have truly believed, not showing off to anyone.

"And establish prayer" means they did not neglect any prayer, as the verb "iqamah" indicates, as was mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Since these two attributes are among the characteristics of Muslims, the meaning becomes: "You only warn the believers." He turned away from evoking them by their most famous titles, despite the brevity that would entail, to evoking them by two relative clauses despite the elaboration in them, in order to use the mention of these two relative clauses as a means of praising them for the sincerity of their faith in belief and action.

The clause "And whoever purifies himself, he purifies only for himself" is a concluding statement functioning as a proverb. Mentioning the concluding statement right after what it concludes indicates that what the concluded statement contains is included in the conclusion from the outset, like the inclusion of the cause of a general ruling within its generality from the first moment, without the general ruling being restricted to it. So the meaning is: those who feared their Lord unseen and established prayer are among those who purified themselves, and they benefited from their purification. Thus the meaning is: only those who fear their Lord unseen benefit from the warning; those are the ones who purified themselves by it, and whoever purifies himself, he purifies only for himself.

The restriction in His saying "﴿he purifies only for himself﴾" is intended to show that their acceptance of the warning was for the benefit of their own souls. It thus contains an allusion that those who paid no heed to his warning abandoned purifying their own souls by it, so their abandonment was a harm to themselves.

The clause "﴿and to Allah is the final return﴾" completes the concluding statement, and the definite article in "al-masir" (the final return) is for the genus, i.e., the entire return is to Allah, equal in it being the return of the one who purifies himself and the return of the one who does not, i.e., each will be recompensed according to what suits him.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in "﴿and to Allah is the final return﴾" is for emphasis, to draw attention that the return is to the One whose glorious name requires attributes suitable for establishing justice and bestowing grace, together with observance of the rhyme (fasila).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verses 19–21:**

﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ ﴿nor are the darknesses and the light﴾ ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ ﴿And the living and the dead are not alike﴾ [Fatir: 22]

These are four similitudes for the believers and the disbelievers, and for faith and disbelief. The disbeliever is likened to the blind man, and disbelief to the darknesses and the scorching heat. The disbeliever is likened to the dead, and the believer is likened to the seeing man, and faith is likened to the light. The believer is likened to the living, a comparison of the intelligible to the perceptible (tashbih al-ma'qul bi'l-mahsus). After he had made clear how little benefit warning brings to the disbelievers, and that only the believers benefit from it, He set forth similitudes for the two groups, uncovering the difference between their two conditions. In these comparisons, their distribution is observed according to the attribute of the disbeliever and the believer, according to the state of disbelief and faith, and according to the effect of faith and the effect of disbelief.

The comparison of the disbeliever's condition and his disbelief was placed before the comparison of the believer's condition and his faith, initially, because the more important purpose of this comparison is to show the horror of the disbeliever's condition, and then to move on to the good condition of its opposite. This comparison came to clarify what the restriction (qasr) in His saying *"You can only warn those who fear their Lord in the unseen"* conveyed, as was mentioned just before, that it is a restriction of the relative kind, a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb). The disbeliever is thus like the blind man in that his affair is mixed between intellect and ignorance, just as the affair of the blind man is mixed between perception and its absence.

The meaning is this: the disbeliever, although he has an intellect by which he perceives matters, his intellect is purely devoted to perceiving the affairs of the worldly life, and it is like nothing in the affairs of the Hereafter, as in His saying, exalted is He: *"They know an outward appearance of the worldly life, but of the Hereafter they are heedless"* (Rum: 7). So his condition, divided between benefiting from the intellect and lacking it, resembles the condition of the blind man in his perceiving some things and not perceiving others.

Blindness is used figuratively to express misguidance. Ibn Rawaha said:

*"He showed us guidance after blindness, so our hearts are certain*
*that what he said is coming to pass."*

Then He likened disbelief to darknesses in that it makes what surrounds the one who is in it not clearly distinguished. For it is among the properties of darkness to conceal things, and the disbeliever has had the ordinary realities hidden from him. Whenever the Qur'an clarifies them for him, he does not move on to something clearer, just as if you described the road to a traveller in the dark.

The word "darknesses" is used in the plural form because that is the more common usage; they do not mention darkness except in the plural form. This was mentioned before in His saying, *"and He made the darknesses and the light"* (al-An'am).

The shade was struck as a similitude for the effect of faith, and its opposite, the scorching heat (al-harur), as a similitude for the effect of disbelief. The shade, in the custom of the first listeners, who were the Arabs, the people of hot lands, which generally seek shade for comfort except during part of the winter season, is a place of comfort. The shade was contrasted with the scorching heat because it is painful and tormenting in their custom, as you know. Its being paired with the scorching heat indicates that the intended meaning is the likening of the believer to the shade in the state of finding it pleasant.

*Al-harur* means the heat of the sun. It is also applied to the hot wind, which is the *samum*; or *al-harur* is the hot wind that blows at night, while the *samum* blows by day.

In this clause, what pertains to the condition of the believers was placed first, contrary to the three preceding clauses, for the sake of harmony with the verse-ending word "*al-harur*." The verse-endings (fawasil) of the Qur'an are among the completions of its eloquence, and so they have a share in its inimitability (i'jaz).

The condition of the believer resembles the shade, in which the feelings are at rest, and in which actions proceed from insight, deliberation and perfection. The condition of the disbeliever resembles the scorching heat, in which souls are agitated, and in which the faculties cannot be settled enough for reflection and insight, and in which opinions and efforts proceed hastily and in disorder.

Know that the construction of the verse is remarkable, for it contains conjunctions (waws al-'atf) and negative particles. Each of the two waws in His saying *"nor the darknesses"* etc., and His saying *"nor the shade"* etc., conjoins a clause to a clause, and conjoins three comparisons, or rather one of them which unites the two groups. The implied sense is: *"the darknesses and the light are not alike, nor are the shade and the scorching heat alike,"* and the implied verb was made explicit at the end in His saying, *"And the living and the dead are not alike."*

As for the three waws in His saying *"and the seeing"* (wal-basir), *"nor the light"* (wa la al-nur), *"nor the scorching heat"* (wa la al-harur), each waw conjoins a single noun to a single noun. So they are six comparisons distributed over each group: *"al-basir"* is conjoined to *"al-a'ma"* (the blind), *"al-nur"* is conjoined to *"al-zulumat"* (the darknesses), and *"al-harur"* is conjoined to *"al-zill"* (the shade). For this reason the negative particle was repeated.

As for the negative particles, two of them are emphatic for the sense of prevalence directed at the two conjoined clauses, whose verbs are omitted: *"nor the darknesses"* and *"nor the shade"*. And two are emphatic for the direction of negation toward the two conjoined single nouns, which are conjoined to two single nouns, in the context of negating equality between them and what they are conjoined to. These are the waw of *"nor the light"* and the waw of *"nor the scorching heat"*. The emphasis is partly by the same thing, which is the particle *la*, and partly by its synonym, which is the particle *ma*. The negative particle was not given in the first negation of equality, because it is the one with which the negation of equality was begun, and the emphasized negation of equality came after it; so it is all a reinforcement of despair. This is a remarkable Qur'anic usage in conjoining negated single words and clauses, and among its instances is His exalted saying, *"Nor are the good deed and the evil deed alike"* (Fussilat: 34), in the surah of Fussilat.

As for the clause *"And the living and the dead are not alike"*, the verb which was implied in the two clauses before it, which is the verb "*yastawi*" (to be alike), was made explicit in this clause, because the similitude here returned to the comparison of the condition of the Muslims and the disbelievers. For it likened the condition of the Muslim to the condition of the living, and the condition of the disbelievers to the condition of the dead. So this is an elevation in the comparison of the two conditions, from likening the believer to the seeing man and the disbeliever to the blind man, to likening the believer to the living and the disbeliever to the dead. Its counterpart in repeating the verb of equality is His saying, exalted is He, in surah al-Ra'd: *"Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Or are the darknesses and the light alike?"* (al-Ra'd: 16).

Since life is the source of all perceptions and efforts, and death is what cuts off perceptions and efforts, faith was likened to life in that the good of this world and the Hereafter springs forth from it, and in receiving and understanding that. Disbelief was likened to death in its cutting off from all beneficial actions and perceptions, and in not receiving what is conveyed to its bearer. So the believer became like the living in a complete resemblance when he came out of disbelief into faith, as if life were breathed into him after death through faith. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, in surah al-An'am: *"Is one who was dead and We gave him life"* (al-An'am: 122). The disbeliever was like the dead as long as he remained in his disbelief.

The comparison of the disbeliever and the believer was mentioned in two places, instead of the comparison of disbelief and faith, and vice versa, because of their mutual implication. The comparison of the disbeliever and the believer was given in two places because the aspect of similarity is clearer in the disbeliever and the believer, and the reverse was done in two places because the aspect of similarity is clearer in the other two places.

The shade was contrasted with the scorching heat because it is painful and tormenting in their custom, as you know. Its being paired with the scorching heat indicates that the intended meaning is the likening of the believer to the shade in the state of finding it pleasant.

*Al-harur* means the heat of the sun. It is also applied to the hot wind, which is the *samum*; or *al-harur* is the hot wind that blows at night, while the *samum* blows by day.

In this clause, what pertains to the condition of the believers was placed first, contrary to the three preceding clauses, for the sake of harmony with the verse-ending word "*al-harur*." The verse-endings (fawasil) of the Qur'an are among the completions of its eloquence, and so they have a share in its inimitability (i'jaz).

The condition of the believer resembles the shade, in which the feelings are at rest, and in which actions proceed from insight, deliberation and perfection. The condition of the disbeliever resembles the scorching heat, in which souls are agitated, and in which the faculties cannot be settled enough for reflection and insight, and in which opinions and efforts proceed hastily and in disorder.

Know that the construction of the verse is remarkable, for it contains conjunctions (waws al-'atf) and negative particles. Each of the two waws in His saying *"nor the darknesses"* etc., and His saying *"nor the shade"* etc., conjoins a clause to a clause, and conjoins three comparisons, or rather one of them which unites the two groups. The implied sense is: *"the darknesses and the light are not alike, nor are the shade and the scorching heat alike,"* and the implied verb was made explicit at the end in His saying, *"And the living and the dead are not alike."*

As for the three waws in His saying *"and the seeing"* (wal-basir), *"nor the light"* (wa la al-nur), *"nor the scorching heat"* (wa la al-harur), each waw conjoins a single noun to a single noun. So they are six comparisons distributed over each group: *"al-basir"* is conjoined to *"al-a'ma"* (the blind), *"al-nur"* is conjoined to *"al-zulumat"* (the darknesses), and *"al-harur"* is conjoined to *"al-zill"* (the shade). For this reason the negative particle was repeated.

As for the negative particles, two of them are emphatic for the sense of prevalence directed at the two conjoined clauses, whose verbs are omitted: *"nor the darknesses"* and *"nor the shade"*. And two are emphatic for the direction of negation toward the two conjoined single nouns, which are conjoined to two single nouns, in the context of negating equality between them and what they are conjoined to. These are the waw of *"nor the light"* and the waw of *"nor the scorching heat"*. The emphasis is partly by the same thing, which is the particle *la*, and partly by its synonym, which is the particle *ma*. The negative particle was not given in the first negation of equality, because it is the one with which the negation of equality was begun, and the emphasized negation of equality came after it; so it is all a reinforcement of despair. This is a remarkable Qur'anic usage in conjoining negated single words and clauses, and among its instances is His exalted saying, *"Nor are the good deed and the evil deed alike"* (Fussilat: 34), in the surah of Fussilat.

As for the clause *"And the living and the dead are not alike"*, the verb which was implied in the two clauses before it, which is the verb "*yastawi*" (to be alike), was made explicit in this clause, because the similitude here returned to the comparison of the condition of the Muslims and the disbelievers. For it likened the condition of the Muslim to the condition of the living, and the condition of the disbelievers to the condition of the dead. So this is an elevation in the comparison of the two conditions, from likening the believer to the seeing man and the disbeliever to the blind man, to likening the believer to the living and the disbeliever to the dead. Its counterpart in repeating the verb of equality is His saying, exalted is He, in surah al-Ra'd: *"Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Or are the darknesses and the light alike?"* (al-Ra'd: 16).

Since life is the source of all perceptions and efforts, and death is what cuts off perceptions and efforts, faith was likened to life in that the good of this world and the Hereafter springs forth from it, and in receiving and understanding that. Disbelief was likened to death in its cutting off from all beneficial actions and perceptions, and in not receiving what is conveyed to its bearer. So the believer became like the living in a complete resemblance when he came out of disbelief into faith, as if life were breathed into him after death through faith. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, in surah al-An'am: *"Is one who was dead and We gave him life"* (al-An'am: 122). The disbeliever was like the dead as long as he remained in his disbelief.

The comparison of the disbeliever and the believer was mentioned in two places, instead of the comparison of disbelief and faith, and vice versa, because of their mutual implication. The comparison of the disbeliever and the believer was given in two places because the aspect of similarity is clearer in the disbeliever and the believer, and the reverse was done in two places because the aspect of similarity is clearer in the other two places.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 22–23:

﴿Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills, but you cannot make hear those who are in the graves.﴾ ﴿You are not but a warner.﴾ Since the greatest deprivation that results from disbelief is the deprivation of benefiting from the most eloquent and truthful speech, which is the Qur'an, the state of the disbeliever became more clearly like death, in that he derives no benefit from the Qur'an and turns away from hearing it. ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may prevail."﴾ [Fussilat: 26]. The state of the believers was the opposite of that, as they received the Qur'an, studied it, and gained understanding of it: ﴿those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom Allah has guided.﴾ The depiction of the state of the believers and disbelievers through the state of the living and the dead was followed by directing the address to the Prophet ﷺ, as an excuse for him regarding the conveying of the message to both groups, and regarding the non-acceptance of his message by one of the two groups, and as consolation for him for the loss of the abundant flow of his counsel in the saline soil of the hearts of the disbelievers. So it was said to him: The acceptance of those who accepted guidance and listened to him was by Allah Most High's preparing their souls to accept the reminder and knowledge, and the non-benefit of those who turned away from that is due to the death of their hearts; they are thus like the dead in the graves, and you cannot make the dead hear. Therefore His saying "Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills, but you cannot make hear those who are in the graves" came in correspondence with His saying "And the living and the dead are not alike," a correspondence of the arrangement known as laff and nashr (interweaving and unfolding in order).

The clause "Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills" is a justification for the clause "You warn only those who fear their Lord in the unseen," because the meaning of restriction (qasr) resolves into affirmation and negation, and so it conveyed two groups: a group that benefited from the warning and a group that did not benefit. This was explained by "Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills."

His saying "but you cannot make hear those who are in the graves" refers to those whom Allah did not will to cause to hear your warning.

"Those who are in the graves" is used figuratively for those whom the warnings did not benefit. He expressed the dead as "those in the graves" because those in the graves are more distant from reaching the voices, since between them and the caller stands the barrier of the earth. This is an elaboration (ītnāb) that conveys a meaning which the concise form would not convey, namely saying: "and you cannot make the dead hear."

The plural forms "al-aḥyā'" (the living) and "al-amwāt" (the dead) were used for variety of expression (tafannun), after the blind and the seeing were mentioned in the singular, because the singular and plural of a noun defined by the definite article of genus (al-jins) are equivalent when the noun has individuals (afrād), unlike "al-nūr" (the light), "al-ẓill" (the shade), and "al-ḥarūr" (the heat). As for the plural of "al-ẓulumāt" (the darknesses), you have already known its reason a moment ago.

The clause "You are not but a warner" conveys a restriction relative to the treatment of making them hear the truth; that is, you are a warner only to those who resemble those in the graves, and you are not one who brings faith into their hearts. This is presented as an excuse for the Prophet ﷺ and consolation for him, since he was concerned about their lack of faith.

The "nadhīr" (warner) is one who announces the expectation of the occurrence of something disliked or painful.

Restricting his description to "warner" is because the context of the speech concerns those who are determined upon disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 24:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner. And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾

This is a resumption of praise for the Prophet ﷺ and an honouring of him through Islam. It also removes the misconception that restricting him to warning is a literal restriction. The point is that his restriction to warning applies to the polytheists whose condition resembled that of the people of the graves. That is, your message combines good news and warning: good news for whoever accepts guidance, and warning for whoever turns away from it. All of this is true, because the recompense follows acceptance. Thus it is a message bound to the truth and to placing things in their proper places.

As for His saying "with the truth" (bi-l-haqq), it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the speaker in "We have sent you," meaning: sending you while We are truthful, not playing. Or it may be from the "kaf" of address, meaning: you are truthful, not lying. Or it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a sending bound to the truth, in which nothing of falsehood mixes. A parallel to this sentence has already occurred in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ is a refutation of the polytheists' view as improbable, that God would send to people a human from among them. That misconception was among the greatest things that barred them from belief. Therefore the proofs of prophethood were followed by the refutation of this barrier-creating doubt, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: "Say: I am not an innovation among the messengers" (Q. 46:9).

Also, in this there is a rebuke to their judgment, since they were content to be below other nations that were honoured with messengers.

The reason for mentioning only the attribute of warner here, without combining it with the attribute of bringer of good news, is to observe the generality in His saying "there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them." Among the nations there are those for whom no good news was obtained, because none of them believed. In the hadith: "The nations were shown to me; a prophet would pass with a group, a prophet would pass with a single man, and a prophet would pass alone," and so on. The prophets who passed alone are those whom none of their people responded to. It may also be that the absence of mention of the attribute of good news is because the context suffices, the indication of what precedes it being sufficient for it. The attribute of warner was chosen for mention because it is more fitting to the situation of addressing the deniers.

The meaning of "nation" (ummah) here is: a great branch of people of a lineage that ends at one common ancestor, uniting many tribes with neighbouring dwelling places, such as the Persian nation, the Roman nation, the Chinese nation, the Indian nation, the Greek nation, the Israelite nation, the Arab nation, and the Berber nation. There is no nation of these but that a warner has passed among it, that is, a messenger or a prophet who warned them of destroying things and the punishment of the Hereafter. Among the warners are those whom We know of, and among them are those who warned and passed away, and whose report has not remained. God, Exalted, said: "And We sent messengers before you; of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you" (Q. 40:78).

The wisdom in warning is that error should not remain current, and that God should bless His servants with the call to the truth, whether they act upon it or not, for it is never free of a good effect upon them. The Qur'an mentioned only the prophets and messengers who were among the Semitic nations dwelling in the lands of Arabia and what bordered them, because when the Qur'an was revealed it began by addressing the Arabs, who had knowledge of these peoples: they knew their reports and witnessed their traces, so that taking lessons from them was more effective. Had the messengers of nations unknown to them been mentioned, their reporting of them would have been mere narration, with no inference or lesson in it.

﴿And if they deny you, those before them also denied. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with the scriptures, and with the illuminating Book.﴾ ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved, and how was My rejection?﴾

The praise of the Prophet ﷺ is followed by consolation (tasliyah) for him concerning his people's denial, and by reassurance that this is the practice of the messengers with their communities.

Since the context of the discourse concerns the communities, the consolation in this verse is framed in terms of the communities' conduct toward their messengers, in the reverse of what appears in the verse of Al 'Imran: ﴿So if they deny you, messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs, the scriptures, and the illuminating Book﴾. This is because the context of the verse of Al 'Imran was the refutation of the attempt by the People of the Book to confound the Messenger, since before it came those who said: ﴿God has covenanted with us that we should not believe a messenger until he brings us an offering consumed by fire﴾.

The style of this verse also differs from that of the verse of Al 'Imran: here each of *al-zubur* (the writings) and *al-kitab al-munir* (the illuminating Book) is linked with the preposition *bi* (with), whereas in the verse of Al 'Imran both are stripped of it. This is because the verse of Al 'Imran came in the context of the Jews' claim that no messenger's miracle should be accepted except the miracle of an offering consumed by fire. So, in refuting their slander, it was said: messengers were denied who each brought various kinds of miracles, such as 'Isa (peace be upon him), and among their miracles were offerings consumed by fire, yet you denied them. Thus the omission of repeating *bi* there indicates that the messengers brought all three kinds.

Since the station here is the consolation of the Messenger ﷺ, it was fitting to mention the trial of the messengers through their communities' denial, according to the differing circumstances of the messengers. Among them were those who came with *ayat* (signs), that is, extraordinary occurrences only, such as Salih, Hud, and Lut. Among them were those who came with *al-zubur*, which are the admonitions that are commanded to be written down and inscribed (*zabr*), that is, set down in writing so that they are preserved and repeated on tongues, such as the Psalms of David and the books of the People of the Book among the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Jeremiah and Elijah. Among them were those who came with *al-kitab al-munir*, meaning the book of laws, such as Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. So the use of *bi* indicates the distribution of kinds of miracles among kinds of messengers.

The *zabur* of Abraham is his scrolls mentioned in God's words: ﴿the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 19].

The *zabur* of Moses is his speech in admonitions that contains no transmission from God, such as his supplication at Qadesh mentioned in chapter nine of the Book of Deuteronomy (Sifr al-Tathniyah), his exhortation at the crossing of the Jordan in chapter twenty-seven of the same book, his hortatory song which he uttered and commanded the Children of Israel to memorize and chant in chapter thirty-two of it, and the supplication with which he blessed the tribes of Israel in the plains of Moab at the end of his life in chapter thirty-three of it.

The *zabur* of Jesus is his sayings reported in the Gospels, which were not ascribed to revelation.

The pronoun in *jaa'uu* (they came) refers to the messengers, and it is distributive: the totality of them came with these kinds of signs. It does not follow that each individual of them came with all of them, just as one says: "the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so."

The answer to *in yukadhdhibuuka* (if they deny you) is omitted, and its cause indicates it, which is His words: ﴿then messengers before you were denied﴾ [Fatir: 4]. The implied meaning is: if they deny you, then do not grieve, and do not think they will escape punishment for that, since the peoples to whom messengers came before these denied, and We punished them for their denial.

The *fa'* in His words "﴿then those before them denied﴾" is an eloquent *fa'* (*fa' fasihah*), or it is a consequence (*tafri'*) upon the omitted clause.

The clause *jaa'at-hum* (their messengers came to them) is a relative clause of *alladhina* (those who), and *min qablihim* (before them) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) of the relative pronoun placed before it, or it is connected to *jaa'at-hum*.

The particle *thumma* (then) conjoins the clause *akhadhtu* (I seized) to the clause *jaa'at-hum*, meaning: then I seized them. *Alladhina kafaruu* (those who disbelieved) is stated explicitly in the place of a pronoun of the third person, to indicate that their seizure was on account of what the relative clause contained, namely that they disbelieved.

The word *akhdh* (seizing) is used metaphorically for annihilation and destruction. Their destruction as recompense for their denial is likened to raiders who attack their enemy, killing them and seizing their wealth, so that their dwellings remain desolate, as though they had been seized from them.

*Kayfa* (how) is an interrogative used to express amazement at their condition, and it is grammatically dependent on *akhadhtu alladhina kafaruu* (I seized those who disbelieved). The meaning is: I seized them with a strange seizure; how do you see its strangeness?

The original use of *kayfa* is to ask about a state. When it is used to express amazement at the condition of their seizure, it necessarily follows that their condition is known, that is, the Prophet ﷺ and everyone whose reports reached them know it. On that well-known knowledge the expression of amazement is built.

*Al-nakir* is a noun for intense disapproval, and here it is a metonymy for intense punishment, because disapproval entails requital for the disapproved act through punishment.

The first-person ya' (the speaker's pronoun ending) is dropped for lightness and for the sake of the rhyme endings (*fawasil*) in pause, since the rhyme endings are regarded in pause. This was discussed in Saba'.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 27:**

﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colours?﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*, a new sentence that begins without a grammatical link to what precedes it) containing an explanation of what came before it: the difference among people in accepting and rejecting guidance, according to what their natures were created to incline toward. Its purpose is to show that difference among the kinds and species is an innate natural order (*nāmūs jabalī*) on which God created the creatures of this earthly world.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, to relieve him of the distress he felt from seeing the disbelievers not benefiting from the Qur'an.

The variation in the outward appearances of individuals within a single kind is presented as an example of the variation in inner natures, to bring the matter closer to understanding. This resumption is therefore an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnāf bayānī*), since such an illustration is something minds crave when they hear His words ﴿Indeed God makes whom He wills hear﴾ (Fatir: 22).

The seeing is visual (*baṣariyya*), and the interrogative is affirmative (*taqrīrī*). The affirmation is expressed through negation, as is customary; I have explained this at His words ﴿Do they not see that it does not speak to them?﴾ (al-A'raf: 148) in Surat al-A'raf and in other verses.

The pronoun in *fa-akhrajnā* ("then We brought forth") is an *iltifāt* (a shift from the third person to the first person).

*Al-alwān* is the plural of *lawn* (colour), which is an accident (*ʿaraḍ*), that is, a quality that appears on the surfaces of bodies. Light shapes it into different qualities according to what results from its reflection to the lenses of the eyes, from a shade resembling darkness, which is the colour black, and a shade resembling dawn, which is the colour white. These are the two origins of colours, and many colours branch out from them, to which conventional and descriptive names have been given. This was discussed at His words ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its colour is"﴾ (al-Baqara: 69) in Surat al-Baqara, and it was discussed in Surat al-Nahl.

The purpose of this reflection is the variation in the colours of kinds within a single species, such as the difference between the colours of apples and quinces, and between the colours of grapes and figs, and the variation in the colours of individuals within a single kind, such as the different colours of dates, olives, grapes, apples and pomegranates.

Mentioning the sending down of water from the sky is an *idmāj* (an incidental embedding) within the main purpose, for the sake of reflection on the power of God, together with what it contains of the unity of the origin of the emergence of the kinds and species, as in His words ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ (al-Ra'd: 4). This is more conducive to reflection.

The two verbal sentences, *anzala* ("sent down") and *akhrajnā* ("brought forth"), are used because the sending down of water and the bringing forth of fruits is continually renewed moment by moment.

The shift from the third person to the first person in *anzala* and *akhrajnā* occurs because the apparent noun (*ism ẓāhir*, here "God") is more suitable to the context of arguing from His power, since it is the name that comprises the meanings of all the attributes.

The first-person pronoun is more suitable to what contains a favour (*imtinān*).

The reflection on the variation in the states of the fruits is placed first because in their variation there is a breadth resembling the breadth of variation among people in their benefits, perceptions and beliefs. A hadith says: "The likeness of the believer who recites the Qur'an is like the citron, its scent is pleasant and its taste is pleasant. The likeness of the believer who does not recite the Qur'an is like the date, its taste is pleasant but it has no scent. The likeness of the hypocrite who recites the Qur'an is like the basil, its scent is pleasant but its taste is bitter. The likeness of the hypocrite who does not recite the Qur'an is like the colocynth, its taste is bitter and it has no scent."

*Mukhtalifan* is stripped of the feminine marker even though its subject (*fāʿil*) is a plural. The rule for a causal descriptive (*naʿt sababī*) is that it agrees with its referent in masculinity or its opposite and in singularity or its opposite, and it does not agree with the noun it qualifies in these respects. Since the subject is a plural of non-rational things, namely the colours, omitting the *tāʾ* in such a case is permissible in usage, and the Qur'an preferred it for the sake of brevity.

The intended meaning of *al-thamarāt* ("the fruits") is the fruits of the date palm, the grape and others. The fruits of the date palm are the most varied in colour, for their colours differ according to their stages of ripening: among them are green, yellow, red and black.

﴿And among the mountains are white and red streaks, varying in colour, and deep black﴾

This is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with the sentence ﴿Do you not see that God﴾, so it is, like it, a new sentence, and its coordination with it is for the evident connection.

*Judadun* ("streaks") is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and *min al-jibāl* ("among the mountains") is its predicate (*khabar*). Placing the predicate first serves to draw attention and to create suspense, so that the subject is mentioned as an incitement to contemplation and reflection.

The *min* here is partitive (*tabʿīḍiyya*), meaning: "and some of the earth of the mountains are streaks." Thus in one mountain there are different streaks, and some streaks may be in some mountains while others are in other mountains.

*Judad* is the plural of *judda* (with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*), which is the path or line in a thing that is clearly visible in it. It is said of the black stripe on a donkey's back that it is a *judda*, and of a gazelle that it has two musk-coloured *juddatān* that separate the colour of its back from the colour of its belly. The white streaks in the mountains are rocks that are white like flint, or that approach whiteness, for some earth becomes like the colour of *al-ahṣab* (a mottled or pale colour), and it is said: "white earth." They do not mean that it is white like lime or gypsum, but that it differs from the usual colours of earth. The red streaks are the red stones in the mountains.

*Gharābīb* is the plural of *ghirbīb*, which is a name for a thing that is intensely black, and no root is known from which it is derived; I suppose it is taken from a non-derived noun, *al-ghurāb* ("the crow"), because of the crow's fame for blackness.

*Sūd* is the plural of *aswad*, which is the one whose colour is black.

The *ghirbīb* indicates something more intense than the meaning of *aswad*. So the apparent arrangement would be for *gharābīb* to come after *sūd*, because the common usage is to say "aswad ghirbīb," just as they say "abyaḍ yaqaq" (very white), "aṣfar fāqiʿ" (intensely yellow) and "aḥmar qānin" (deep red), and they do not say "ghirbīb aswad." This arrangement was departed from for the sake of observing the rhyme (*fawāṣil*) based on the quiescent *wāw* and *yāʾ*, beginning from His words ﴿And God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ (Fatir: 15). Moreover, the claim that *gharībun* is a modifier following *aswad* is open to consideration, and the verse supports this consideration. The claim that *gharābīb* is an attribute of a deleted noun indicated by *sūd* is evidently forced, and likewise the claim of al-Farra' that the speech is in inverted order (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*). The purpose of emphasis is achieved in every case.

[Page 304]

﴿And among mankind, the creatures, and the cattle are those of diverse colours.﴾ Its position is like that of His saying, ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of diverse hues﴾ [Fatir: 27]. It does not follow that the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun (nakira) must have no other meaning, since the fronting of the predicate here is what justified beginning with the indefinite noun.

The diversity of human colours is a general diversity, namely the colours of the categories of humankind, which are white, black, yellow and red according to the geographical classification. The Arabs have another classification of the colours of human categories in their speech, which was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿And the difference of your tongues and your colours﴾ [al-Rum: 22] in Surat al-Rum.

The "min" (from/among) is partitive (tab'idiyya). The meaning is that those whose colours differ are a part of mankind, and the totality of the differing things is all of mankind, and likewise the creatures and the cattle. This is a precise arrangement, which brevity (al-ijaz) called for.

In the clause ﴿And among the mountains are streaks﴾ [Fatir: 27] and ﴿And among mankind, the creatures, and the cattle are those of diverse colours﴾ the nominal form (al-ismiyya) is used rather than the verbal form (al-fi'liyya), as in the preceding clause, because the diversity of the colours of the mountains and of the animals, which indicates the diversity of the states of creation, is a constant diversity that does not change, whereas it occurs only once, at creation, and at the generation of offspring.
