﴿Likewise, only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God. Indeed God is Almighty, Oft-Forgiving.﴾ My clearer view is that "kadhalika" (likewise) is the beginning of a statement that stands in the place of reporting the conclusion after the mention of the evidence. The meaning is: likewise is the matter of difference in the outward aspects of things, observed in the difference of their colours, and this is a preparation for what follows of the detailed deduction in His saying, ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾, that is, only those among the humans, whose colours differ, who have knowledge fear God. So the clause ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ is a resumptive clause (musta'nafa) relative to the clause "kadhalika". When this is known, it indicates by implication that those who are not men of knowledge cannot attain the fear of God, and so it shows that humans differ in the states of their hearts and their faculties of perception. This is like His saying, ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18].

This mode of indication was chosen in order to single out the people of knowledge and faith for honour, so that the discourse may move on to the detail of this in His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of God﴾ [Fatir: 29], and so on.

So His saying "kadhalika" is the predicate of an omitted subject, which the context indicates. The estimated sense is: "likewise the difference" or "likewise the matter", following the manner of His exalted saying in Surat al-Kahf, ﴿Thus it was; and We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ [al-Kahf: 91], which is among the decisive statements (fasl al-khitab), as you have learned there. For this reason it is good to pause on what precedes it and to begin afresh with what follows.

As for making "kadhalika" a dependent of the preceding speech, this does not suit the arrangement of the Qur'an, because it is weak.

The restriction (qasr) derived from "innama" (only) is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), that is, those who are ignorant, namely the people of polytheism, do not fear Him. For among their most distinctive attributes is that they are the people of ignorance (al-jahiliyya), that is, the lack of knowledge. So the believers at that time were the men of knowledge, and the polytheists were the ignorant, from whom the fear of God is negated. Then, the men of knowledge vary greatly in degrees of fear. The fronting of the object of "yakhsha" (fears) before its subject is because those in whom the fear of God is restricted are the men of knowledge, so it was necessary to place it later, following the custom of placing the restricted element later.

The men of knowledge intended here are those who know God and the Sharia (the sacred law), and the fear grows in proportion to the knowledge of this. As for those who have knowledge of sciences not connected with knowing God, His reward, and His punishment, with knowledge in its proper form, their knowledge does not bring them closer to the fear of God. This is because the one who knows the Sharia is not confused about the realities of the legal terms (al-asma' al-shar'iyya); he understands their places correctly, observes them in their places, and knows their consequences, whether good or bad. So he does what carries God's intent and the aim of His law, and abstains from what does not. If he opposes what the Sharia calls for in some circumstances or at some times, out of the pull of desire, whim, or the hastening of worldly gain, he remains in that state of opposition certain that he is entangled in something whose outcome is not praiseworthy. That certainty does not linger long before it turns him away from persisting in opposition, by giving it up or reducing it.

A non-scholar, if he is guided by the scholars, his striving is like the striving of the scholars and his fear arises from the fear of the scholars. Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd said: "Knowledge is a guide to good things and a leader towards them, and the nearest of the scholars to God are those most in His favour, most fearful of Him, and most desirous of what is with Him."

The clause ﴿Indeed God is Almighty, Oft-Forgiving﴾ completes the indication of God's self-sufficiency (istighna') from the faith of the polytheists, while He still desires good for them. Since this attribute contains a kind of turning away from them, which may produce despair in the souls of those near to them, the heart is reconciled by following the attribute "Almighty" with the attribute "Oft-Forgiving", meaning that He accepts repentance from them if they turn to what God has called them to. Moreover, in the attribute "Oft-Forgiving" there is great benefit for one of the two sides of the restriction, namely the scholars, that is, He is Oft-Forgiving towards them.

This is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that elaborates what precedes it) explaining the statement ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28], so ﴿those who recite the Book of God﴾ are the ones meant by "those who have knowledge." It moves on to explain the success of the believers who followed the Reminder and feared the Most Merciful in the unseen, since their state is the opposite of those who did not hear the Qur'an and, when reminded of it, were like the people of the graves who hear nothing. Having first praised them in general terms with the words ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28], and having summarised the goodness of their reward by mentioning the attribute "Forgiving," this verse ends with ﴿Indeed, He is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾, so that this praise is detailed and its effects and benefits are mentioned.

[Page 306]

The meaning of ﴿those who recite the Book of God﴾ is those who believe in it, because they are known and recognised for this, and they are the ones meant by "those who have knowledge." God says: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 49]. This is also a metonymy (*kinaya*) for their faith, because no one recites the Book except one who affirms it and receives it with care. This implies that they acquire Sacred Knowledge of doctrines, morals and obligations. The present tense verb indicates the continual renewal of their recitation, since the revelation of the Qur'an is ongoing: whenever a portion of it is revealed, they receive it and study it.

"The Book of God" is the Qur'an. It departs from its proper name to the generic noun construct attached to the Divine Name (Allah), because this attachment conveys the exaltation of its status.

After what is the sign of acceptance of faith and of knowledge of it, the verse follows with another sign, which is the establishment of prayer, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿who believe in the unseen and establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. Prayer is the greatest of bodily acts. Then it is followed by a great act concerning wealth, which is spending (*infaq*). By "spending," wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, is meant charity, both obligatory and recommended. The word "spending" does not occur in the Meccan surahs except with the meaning of recommended charity, since the zakat had not yet been prescribed at that time. Moreover, charity may be obligatory without a fixed minimum or specified amount, and later it was specified by the threshold (*nisab*) and fixed quantities.

The past tense verbs are used for establishing prayer and spending because the obligation of prayer and charity has been established and they act upon it, so there is no renewal in this. Compliance with what they were charged with implies that they are constant in it.

His saying ﴿of what We have provided them﴾ is an embedding (*idmaj*) of a reminder of God's favour, and an allusion that it is spending out of gratitude for God's blessing upon them in provision, so they give from it to those in need. A shift (*iltifat*) occurs from the third person in ﴿the Book of God﴾ to the first person plural in ﴿of what We have provided them﴾, because the first person suits the reminder of favour.

[Page 307]

The words ﴿secretly and openly﴾ are in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun after "spent," meaning spending in secret and spending in public. The verbal noun specifies the type.

The meaning is that they seek by spending nothing but God's good pleasure; they do not show off with it. They spend where no one sees them, and they spend in the sight of people, and the sight of people does not prevent them from spending.

Placing "secretly" first indicates that it is more excellent, since the taint of showing off is absent from it. Mentioning "openly" indicates that the sight of the polytheists does not prevent them from spending; they have openly declared their faith and its laws, loving whoever loves it and disliking whoever dislikes it.

﴿They hope for a commerce﴾ is the predicate of "indeed" (*inna*).

The predicate is used in the sense of a glad tidings (*insha' al-tabshir*), as if it were said: "Let them hope for a commerce." The causal clause ﴿so that He may pay them their wages in full﴾ strengthens this as an indication that the sense is one of glad tidings.

"Commerce" is a metaphor for their deeds of recitation, prayer and spending. The point of resemblance is the similarity between the reward being due for their deeds and the profit being due from trade.

The meaning is: let them hope that their deeds will be like a profitable trade.

"Ruin" (*bawar*) is destruction, and the destruction of trade is the loss of the merchant. So the meaning of ﴿it will never be ruined﴾ is that it is profitable. ﴿It will never be ruined﴾ is an attribute of "commerce," and the meaning is that they hope for the non-ruin of the commerce.

The attribute is thus the basis of the glad tidings and of the hope, not the very essence of commerce, because the resemblance of a dreadful act to the act of a merchant is something well known.

The phrase ﴿so that He may pay them﴾ is connected to "they hope," meaning: We gave them this glad tiding and decreed it for them, so that We may pay them their wages. A shift occurs from the first person in ﴿of what We have provided them﴾ to the third person, returning to the context of the third person in ﴿recite the Book of God﴾, meaning: so that God may pay those who recite His Book.

"Payment" (*tawfiya*) is making a thing complete, that is, whole, with no deficiency or loss in it.

He records for them the bounty, in that He increases their reward beyond what their deeds deserve, out of His bounty

[Page 308]

that is, His generosity, namely the multiplication of good deeds mentioned in His saying: ﴿like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261].

This promise is concluded with what confirms it: forgiveness and appreciation are among His attributes, for among His attributes are "the Forgiving, the Appreciative," that is, the one who forgives much and is greatly appreciative.

Forgiveness applies to the shortcomings of obedient servants, for the true obedience to God, which lies in the heart, in deeds and in thoughts, can never be fully discharged except by the infallible. But God has overlooked for the community what its souls whisper and what it intended but did not do, as well as minor lapses, and the erasure of past sins through repentance. He appreciates by action, because the one who rewards a deed done by the doer with ample recompense shows by his recompense that he approves of the doer's act.

This statement is emphasised with the particle of emphasis, for added certainty, and because emphasis indicates that this is the cause of the full payment of wages and their increase.

﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming what is before it.﴾ Since the beginning of this passage mentioned, among the causes of the believers' reward, their recitation of the Book of Allah, the praise of them was followed by praise of the Qur'an, as a reminder of that. Moreover, in reminding of the majesty and nobility of the Qur'an there is an allusion to the reason why those who recite it deserve what they deserve. Its praise began with the statement that it is a revelation from Allah to His Messenger, and this relation alone is sufficient praise of the Book. It also contains praise of the one to whom it was sent, from the words ﴿And that which We have revealed to you﴾. In this there is a joy for the Prophet (ﷺ) and good news to him that he is the best of the messengers and that his Book is the best of books.

This is the rhetorical point of referring to the predicate's subject by the relative pronoun (al-ism al-mawsul), because of the allusion in the relative clause to the reason why it is the complete truth, rather than using a pronoun, which would be what the apparent structure requires, as in saying: "And it is the true Book."

The definite article in "al-Kitab" is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd).

The word "min" (مِن) is explanatory (bayaniyyah), clarifying the vagueness of the relative pronoun. The sense is: "And the Book which We have revealed to you is the truth." The relative clause, which should properly stand as a qualifier of "al-Kitab," is placed first to create suspense through its vagueness, so that the detail that follows settles more firmly in the mind.

Thus the clause ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾ [Fatir: 29], and is therefore in the same position as it, in the sense of a resumed statement (isti'naf). The pronoun "huwa" (هو) is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and it emphasises the restriction (qasr) implied by the definiteness of the predicate.

The definite article in "al-Haqq" is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). The definiteness of both parts restricts the predicate to the subject (qasr al-musnad 'ala al-musnad ilayh), that is, it restricts the genus of truth to ﴿that which We have revealed to you﴾. This is a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i), for emphasis, since the truthfulness of other books is not taken into account.

As for non-divine books, such as the Zand-Fista, the book of Zaradusht (Zoroaster), and the books of the Sabians, the reason is that the little truth in them has been submerged by falsehood and illusions.

As for the divine books, such as the Torah and the Gospel, and what the books of the prophets contain, such as the Psalms (al-Zabur) and the Book of Irmiya (Jeremiah), from divine revelation: whatever the Qur'an has testified to its truthfulness has entered into the testimony of His words ﴿confirming what is before it﴾. Whatever has been abrogated (naskh) by the Qur'an, the abrogation has clarified the limit of its validity in the Qur'an. This too is a confirmation of those books, because it removes the false impression of their invalidity for one who finds their contradiction in the Qur'an. Whatever may have been transmitted with distortion or misinterpretation has entered what the restriction excluded. The Qur'an has clarified most of it and revealed its places, as in His words ﴿And it was forbidden to you to expel them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85].

The meaning of "ma bayna yadayhi" (what is before it) is what preceded it, because what precedes comes forward before what it precedes, so it is as though it walks between its hands, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾ [Saba': 46].

[Page 310]

What is meant by "ma bayna yadayhi" is what came before it of the sacred laws (shara'i'), the most important of which are the law of Musa and the law of 'Isa, peace be upon them both.

"Mussaddiqan" (مُصَدِّقًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-Kitab," and the governing verb of the circumstantial qualifier is "awhayna" (أوحينا). This is to convey that, although it is truth in the highest degree, it confirms the true books and affirms what they contain of truth.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with His servants, Seeing.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) that comprehends what the verses before it contained: the preference of some of Allah's servants over others, the hidden states of their hearts with regard to fear of Allah or its absence, the turning of some of them to acts of obedience and the aversion of others, and the preference of some of Allah's books over others, which likewise implies the preference of some messengers over others by them. The placement of the words ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with His servants, Seeing﴾ is to persuade the listeners that Allah has knowledge of His servants, and He treats them according to what He knows of them, and He chooses from among them the one whom He knows to be fit for His choosing. By this He silenced those who said ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8], and likewise those people of the Book who deny the Qur'an on the grounds that it came to invalidate their Book.

"Khabir" (الخبير) means one who knows the subtleties of matters, both intelligible and perceptible, both apparent and hidden.

"Basir" (البصير) means one who knows matters that are seen. The placement of "Khabir" before "Basir" is because it is more comprehensive. The mention of "Basir" after it is for attention to deeds, which are among the things seen, and which are the majority of the sacred laws of Islam. The pairing of "Khabir" with "Basir" has been repeated in many places in the Qur'an.

The emphasis by "inna" (إنّ) and the lam is for the sake of giving importance to the intended meaning of this statement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 32:

﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants. Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who outstrips others in good deeds, by Allah's permission. That is the great bounty.﴾

"Thumma" (then) here indicates a graded sequence (al-tartib al-rutbi), as is its usual function when it conjoins sentences. Here it is used to conjoin sentences by way of mention (al-'atf al-dhikri), so the sentences it links are treated as if they were newly begun. This sentence is therefore like a fresh beginning, and "thumma" marks an ascent in the new beginning. This is an ascent in extolling the Qur'an, which includes extolling the Messenger (ﷺ), and a rising in his joy and good tidings. After he was reminded of the excellence of his Book, a matter already established for him, he was given further good tidings of the enduring of his Book and of its being given to a community who are the chosen ones among the servants of Allah the Exalted, and good tidings that they act upon it and do not abandon it as earlier nations abandoned their books and messengers, in accordance with His saying ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, to the end of the verse. This good tiding was more important to the Prophet (ﷺ) than the information that the Qur'an is true and confirms what lies before it, because this good tiding was not known to him, so its impact was greater.

Al-Zamakhshari took "thumma" here to indicate temporal sequence (al-tarakhi al-zamani), and so he needed to strain to establish the meaning.

By "al-Kitab" (the Book) is meant the well-known Book, which was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book﴾ [Fatir: 31], namely the Qur'an.

"Awrathna" means "We made [them] inheritors." One says "waritha" when the property of a close deceased person comes to him. It is also used in the sense of acquiring without earning or exchange, so its meaning would be: We made them those who take the Book from Us. Or we may take "inheritance" as used in the sense of instruction to receive, i.e., We commanded the Muslims to inherit the Qur'an, that is, to receive it from the Messenger (ﷺ). On both possibilities, inheritance carries the meaning of giving, so the verb "awrathna" is rightly transitive to two objects. The apparent arrangement would have been that the first object, which is the recipient in meaning, be the first object and the other the second. This was deliberately reversed here, placing the second object first, because there is no risk of ambiguity, for the sake of emphasis on the Book being given. As for the extolling of those who take the Book, this has been achieved through the relative clause.

By "those whom Allah chose" is meant the believers, as the Exalted said ﴿O you who believe, bow down and prostrate yourselves﴾ [al-Hajj: 77] up to His saying ﴿He has chosen you﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Allah chose for faith and Islam the best community among the people. Many hadiths supporting this meaning have been transmitted in the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, which Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir.

Since it was intended to generalize the good tiding while clarifying that they are of ranks in what they were given good tidings of, the division was introduced with His saying ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ to the end. It is therefore an elaboration of the ranks of the chosen ones, so that the good tiding encompasses all their categories, and it should not be supposed that the one who wrongs himself is deprived of it. The criterion of being chosen is faith and Islam, which is submission in speech and surrender.

In the division, the mention of the one who wrongs himself was placed first, to remove the suspicion that he is deprived of Paradise, and to hasten his joy.

The "fa" in His saying ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ etc. is an elaboration of the states of those who were given the Book, i.e., those who were given the Qur'an. The pronoun in "minhum" most apparently refers to ﴿those whom We chose﴾, and this is the view of al-Hasan; accordingly, the one who wrongs himself is among the chosen. It has been said that it refers to "Our servants" in general, i.e., "and among Our servants in absolute terms." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada and al-Dahhak; accordingly, the one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever. The effect of this disagreement extends to the interpretation of the pronoun in ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter﴾ [Fatir: 33], and for this reason al-Hasan's view accords with what was reported from 'Umar, 'Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda, 'Uqba ibn 'Amr, and what is reported from 'A'isha, and it is the preponderant view.

Those who wrong themselves are those who drag themselves into committing sin, for a person's disobedience to his Lord is a wronging of himself, because he exposes himself to the specific punishment for sins in its details. That is a wronging of the self because it is an transgression against it, since he has deprived it of some good, little or much, and exposed it to what it will find the requital of its blameworthy act. The Exalted said, relating about Adam and Eve when they disobeyed what they had been forbidden from eating of the tree, ﴿They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves"﴾ [al-A'raf: 23], and He said ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness of Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa: 110], and He said ﴿Except one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil, indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Naml: 11] in Surat al-Naml, and He said ﴿Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins"﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] in Surat al-Zumar.

The lam in "li-nafsihi" is the lam of reinforcement, because the operating word is a derivative in its action, being an active participle.

Al-Muqtasid (the moderate) is the one other than he who wrongs himself, as the contrast requires. They are those who avoid the major sins and did not deprive themselves of the commanded good, though they may commit minor faults (al-lamam) that Allah pardons, and they did not attain the utmost of the acts of drawing near which raise ranks. Thus al-iqtisad is an ifti'al form from al-qasd, which is the carrying out of moderation (al-qasd), namely the middle between two extremes, as determined by context. When it is mentioned here in contrast to the one who wrongs himself and the foremost, it is known that he is in a state between these two states; he is neither a wrongdoer to himself nor foremost.

Al-sabiq (the foremost), its origin is: one who reaches a specific goal before others who walk toward it. Here it is used figuratively for obtaining excellence, since the foremost wins the prize ("sabq," with a fatha on the ba'), or it is figurative for exerting effort to attain Allah's pleasure. On both figurative considerations, it is a metonymy for increasing in good, since precedence entails quickening steps, and quickening is abundance. In this precedence there is also variation, like horses in a race.

Al-khayrat (good deeds) is the plural of khayr in an irregular pattern; khayr means beneficial. Here it means acts of obedience, because they are righteous deeds beneficial to their doer and to people through their effects.

The ba' here is for location, i.e., "in good deeds," as in His saying ﴿They hasten to sin and aggression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 62].

The mention of good deeds in the other category indicates that they are intended in the first two categories too, so it returns to the meaning "one who wrongs himself in good deeds" and "moderate in good deeds" as well. You may also take the meaning of "one who wrongs himself" as falling short of them in good deeds, as in His saying ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not wrong anything of it﴾ [al-Kahf: 33], i.e., did not fall short of its customary fruiting, in Surat al-Kahf.

The "idhn" (permission) is used in the sense of facilitation by way of metaphor, and the ba' is causal, attached to "sabiq." What is meant is not a command, because Allah commanded all people to do good, whether or not they did it or fell short in it.

You may also take the ba' as accompaniment and make it a stable adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to "sabiq," i.e., "foremost, accompanied by Allah's permission," and "idhn" would be a verbal noun in the sense of the object, i.e., a foremost one accompanied by what Allah has permitted, i.e., he did not oppose it.

On the first reading, it is an extolling of the foremost, that their precedence came with help from Allah and facilitation from Him.

Among what you have seen of the interpretation of these three ranks in the verse, taken from the words of the scholars,

with an addition that cannot be dispensed with, one does not need to wander in its wildernesses; there are many sayings on its interpretation that exceeded forty.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿That is the great bounty﴾ refers to the being chosen understood from ﴿We chose﴾, or to what was mentioned of choosing and inheriting the Book.

Al-fadl (bounty) is increase in good, and "al-kabir" (great) is meant as possessing moral greatness, which is nobility, namely the bounty of coming out of disbelief into faith and Islam. This bounty has ranks in nobility, as indicated by dividing its people into wrongdoer, moderate, and foremost. The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) serves to emphasize the restriction arising from the definition of the two parts, and it is real restriction, because the great bounty is confined to what is pointed to by that, since every bounty other than that is not great.

The reason for this confinement is that this choosing and inheritance of the Book combined the excellence of this world and the bounty of the Hereafter. The Exalted said ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and He said ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth, as He made successors those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely substitute for them, after their fear, security﴾ [al-Nur: 55].

﴿Gardens of Eden, which they will enter. Therein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾

The most apparent view is that it is a *badal ishtimal* (an apposition of inclusion) to His words ﴿That is the great bounty﴾ [Fatir: 32], since entering the Garden is among the things that the bounty comprises, as you know. The singling out of this bounty from among its kinds is because it is the greatest of bounties, and because it is a sign of Allah's good pleasure with them when they enter the Garden, ﴿and the good pleasure of Allah is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

It is also permissible that it be an *istinaf bayani* (an explanatory resumption) explaining the great bounty, which has been explained by its greatest kind. The meaning is one.

The plural pronoun in "yadkhulunaha" (they enter it) refers back to ﴿those whom We have chosen﴾ [Fatir: 32], which is divided into three categories: the one who wrongs himself, the one who is moderate, and the one who is foremost in good deeds. That is, all of these will enter the Garden, because all the believers will ultimately reach the Garden, as the widely transmitted reports indicate. Al-Tirmidhi has related, with a chain containing two unknown narrators, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning this verse, ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants; of them is one who wrongs himself, and of them is one who is moderate, and of them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32], "They are all of one rank, and they are all in the Garden." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith (a hadith narrated by a single chain at some level), which we do not know except through this route." Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said in *al-'Arida*: "Some people have said that these three categories are those mentioned in Surat al-Waqi'ah: the companions of the right hand, the companions of the left hand, and the foremost. This is false, because the companions of the left hand are in the blazing Fire, whereas the people of Surat Fatir are in a lofty Garden. Allah mentioned them between an opening and a closing. As for the opening, it is His words ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾ [Fatir: 32], so He made them chosen. Then He said at the end concerning them, ﴿Gardens of Eden, which they will enter﴾, and none is chosen except one who enters the Garden. But among the people of the Garden there is one who wrongs himself, so He said, ﴿of them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fatir: 32]. The one who wrongs himself is the disobedient, whereas the absolute wrongdoer is the disbeliever. It was said of the first (the one who wrongs himself) out of gentleness toward him, and it was said of the other, the one foremost in good deeds by Allah's permission, to indicate that this is by Allah's blessing and bounty, and not from the condition of the servant." End of quotation.

In the reporting of the predicate by a verbal predicate about the subject, there is a benefit that strengthens the judgment. The verb is formed in the present tense (*mudari'*) because it refers to the future. Likewise is the form of "yuhallawna" (they will be adorned), which is a second predicate concerning ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. Its parallel has preceded in Surat al-Hajj, so refer to it there.

Nafi', 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read "wa lu'lu'an" (and pearls) in the accusative, as a conjunction upon the position (*mahall*) of "asawir" (bracelets). This is because, when it is put in the genitive by the redundant preposition, it occupies the position of the accusative as the second object of the verb "yuhallawna". Thus it is permissible for the conjoined word to be put in the accusative, observing the position of the word it is conjoined to. The rest of the readers read it in the genitive, observing the wording (*lafz*). Both are valid readings.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 35, verses 34–35:

﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative."﴾ ﴿He who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty; no fatigue touches us therein, nor does weariness touch us therein.﴾

The most apparent view is that the clause "wa-qālū" (وقالوا, "and they say") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the main action) relating to the pronoun in "yuḥallawna" (يُحَلَّوْنَ, "they will be adorned"). This avoids the need to interpret the past tense as expressing certainty of occurrence, although he did not intend that in His saying "yadkhulūnahā" (يَدْخُلُونَها, "they will enter it"). That statement coincides with the adornment and the dressing, and it is a speech that passes among them at that moment, to express praise of Allah for what He granted them of entering Paradise, and for the honour contained in it.

The removal of grief (idhhāb al-ḥazan) is a figurative usage (majāz) for being delivered from it. Thus, its removal is true after it has occurred, and it is also true when it has not occurred.

Al-ḥazan (الحَزَنُ) is sorrow. The meaning is that when they were given what they were given, what they had been in before of the terror of the standing place and the fear of punishment, relative to the foremost (al-sābiqūn) and the moderate (al-muqtaṣidūn), and what they had been in of punishment, relative to those who wronged themselves, was removed from them.

The clause ﴿Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ is a resumptive praise (istiʾnāf, a new sentence that begins afresh without grammatical connection to what precedes it) to Allah, by which they gave thanks for the blessing of safety. They praised Him for forgiveness, since He overlooked what they had committed of minor sins (al-lamam), passing thoughts of the soul (ḥadīth al-anfus), and similar things, relative to the moderate and the foremost, and for what He overlooked of prolonged punishment and the acceptance of intercession, relative to the varying states of those who wronged themselves. They also praised Allah as "Appreciative" (shakūr), because they saw His pouring out of good upon them and the multiplying of good deeds beyond their righteous works. This is in the manner of what preceded in His saying: ﴿That He may give them their rewards and increase them of His bounty. Indeed, He is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ [Fāṭir: 30].

Al-muqāmah (الْمُقامَةُ) is a masdar mīmī (a verbal noun formed with a prefixed mīm, from the root meaning to stay) from "aqāma bil-makān" (to reside in a place) when one settles in it. The intended meaning is the abode of eternity. ﴿The abode of permanence﴾ is in the accusative as the second object of ﴿He settled us﴾ (aḥallanā), meaning "He made us dwell."

The "min" (مِن) in His saying ﴿by His bounty﴾ [Fāṭir: 30] is a min of origin (ibtidāʾiyyah), in the position of a circumstantial clause describing ﴿the abode of permanence﴾.

Al-faḍl (الفَضْلُ) is bestowal, and it is the brother of tafaddul (favour) in that it is a gift from Him and a generosity.

Among the bounty of Allah is that He made Paradise a reward for righteous deeds, because if He had willed, He would not have made any bestowal for righteous acts, and their reward would have been merely safety from punishment. The matter of one who did not deserve eternal abiding in the Fire would have been an even balance, meaning neither punishment nor reward, so he would remain like the grazing beasts. They only meant by this the completeness of thanks and the utmost in courtesy.

The clause ﴿no fatigue touches us therein﴾ is a second circumstantial clause.

Al-massu (المَسُّ) is reaching, at the beginning of its occurrence, and al-naṣab (النَّصَبُ) is toil, such as from intense heat or intense cold. Al-lughūb (اللُّغُوبُ) is exhaustion resulting from labour or running.

The repetition of the negated verb in His saying ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾ is for emphasis on the negation of touching.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 36:

﴿And those who disbelieve, for them is the fire of Hell. It will not be decreed for them so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one.﴾

The juxtaposition of the three categories of those to whom the Book was inherited with the mention of the disbelievers increases our certainty that those categories are the categories of the believers, and the juxtaposition of the recompense of the disbelievers with the fire of Hell makes clear that Paradise is the abode of the three categories, though with variation in time and place.

In His words, exalted is He, concerning the disbelievers, ﴿nor will its punishment be lightened for them﴾, there is an allusion to the fact that the fire of the punishment of the believers is distinct from the fire of the polytheists.

The clause ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ is coordinated (ma'tufah) upon the clause ﴿Gardens of Eden, they will enter them﴾ [Fatir: 33].

The statement about the fire of Hell, that it is "for them" (lahum), is expressed with the lam of entitlement (lam al-istihqaq), to indicate that it has been prepared as the recompense for their deeds, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His words ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 131] in Surat Al 'Imran. Thus the fire of the punishment of the sinful believers is a different fire, or it was prepared for the disbelievers.

Those believers who wronged themselves and were admitted into it entered it only because of their committing evil deeds, which by their nature are fitting for the disbelievers.

The prepositional phrase in ﴿for them is the fire of Hell﴾ is fronted before the predicate's subject, so that when the listeners hear it, it settles in their souls with complete settling.

The clause ﴿It will not be decreed for them﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause ﴿for them is the fire of Hell﴾. Al-qada' (decree) in its essential meaning is judgment, and from it is the qada' of Allah, meaning His judgment and what He brings into existence among His creatures. It may also be used in the sense of causing death, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So Musa struck him and caused his death﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]; and here it is open to the literal meaning, i.e., Allah does not decree their death, so His words "so that they die" are a consequence of the decree. The meaning is: it will not be decreed upon them with death so that they die. It is also open to the figurative meaning, which is death. The sequencing of "so that they die" upon this interpretation is that they will not die except with the kind of causing death upon which the true death follows, at which sensation ceases; it thus conveys that they will die a death in which there is nothing of death except its pains, without its relief. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And they will call out, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain.">[az-Zukhruf: 77] and He, exalted is He, said ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment﴾ [an-Nisa': 56].

The pronoun in "its punishment" refers to Hell, so as to include what has been reported: that the condemned are punished by the Fire, and are punished by az-Zamharir, which is the intensity of cold, and all of that is from the punishment of Hell.

The phrase "thus" (kadhalika) occupies the position of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) for "najzi" (We recompense), i.e., We recompense them with a recompense like that recompense. This was discussed previously at His words, exalted is He, ﴿And thus We made you a midmost nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one﴾ is a concluding summation (tadhyil). Al-kafur: the one intensely in disbelief, and this is the polytheist.

The majority read "najzi" with the nun of majesty and "kull" in the accusative, while Abu 'Amr alone read "yujza" with the yā' of the third person and the passive form, with "kull" in the nominative.

The pronoun refers to those who disbelieved, and the sentence is coordinated (*ʿatf*) with the sentence ﴿For them is the Fire of Hell﴾ [Fatir: 36]. It is not made a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), because the concluding statement (*tadhyīl*) signals the end of the speech and the beginning of a new one.

﴿They will cry out therein﴾: *yaṣṭarikhūna* is an intensive form of *yaṣrukhūna*. It is a *iftiʿāl* form derived from *al-ṣurākh*, which means shouting with great force and effort, so *al-iṣṭirākh* intensifies it. The meaning is that they shout because of the severity of what has befallen them.

The clause ﴿Our Lord, bring us out﴾ explains the clause ﴿they will cry out﴾. They think that raising their voices brings them closer to God's knowledge of their call, and it shows that they cannot bear what they are in.

Their saying ﴿we will do righteous deeds﴾ is a promise to make up for the righteous deeds they missed, but it is repentance after its time has passed.

Because the promise is intended, ﴿we will do﴾ (*naʿmal*) is in the jussive mood as the answer to the supplication. The implied meaning is: "If You bring us out, we will do righteous deeds."

﴿other than what we used to do﴾ is an adjectival qualifier (*naʿt*) of *ṣāliḥan* (righteous). The meaning is: a deed different from what we used to do in the world. This is regret for what they used to do, because they have come to know with certainty that their deeds were corrupt and harmful, for that realm is the realm of realities.

* * *

﴿Did We not give you long life, in which whoever would take heed could take heed? And the warner came to you. So taste (it), for the wrongdoers have no helper.﴾

The *waw* coordinates an implied verb of saying, which is understood from the context in the pronoun of ﴿We gave you long life﴾, and it is coordinated with the sentence ﴿they will cry out therein﴾, since their crying out is speech from them. The implied meaning is: they say, "Our Lord, bring us out," and We say, "Did We not give you long life?"

The interrogative is a rebuke (*taqrīʿ*) for reproach. The affirmation is expressed in the form of a negation, as a preparation so that the one being addressed will deny it, and then when he says "Yes," it is known that he could not deny it, even though the ground for denial had been prepared for him.

*Al-taʿmīr* means prolonging life. It has been discussed more than once before, including at the words ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at the words ﴿nor is any aged person given long life, nor is anything reduced from his lifespan﴾ [Fatir: 11] in this surah.

*Mā* is a temporal verbal (*maṣdariyya*) particle, meaning the period of a person's being given long life.

The clause ﴿in which whoever would take heed could take heed﴾ is a qualifier of *mā*, meaning a period long enough in its extent for remembrance and insight.

*Al-nadhīr* (the warner) is the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). The clause ﴿the warner came to you﴾ is coordinated with the clause "Did We not give you long life," because its meaning is a statement of fact, so a statement of fact is coordinated with it. This is because coordinating a statement (*khabar*) with a command or question (*inshāʾ*) is permissible according to the verified view, and it is good here.

The Messenger is described as the warner because what matters most about him in relation to them is warning.

The *fāʾ* in ﴿so taste﴾ is for consequence (*tafrīʿ*). The object of *dhūqū* (taste) is omitted because the context indicates it, meaning: taste the punishment.

The imperative in ﴿so taste﴾ is used to mean continuity, and it is a metonymy (*kināya*) for not being released from the punishment.

His saying ﴿so the wrongdoers have no helper﴾ is a consequence of what came before in the narration. It may be part of the speech with which God rebuked them, so it is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*) to it and a consequence of it, to make them despair of release. The meaning is: where are those whom you claimed to be your allies and helpers? For you have no helper.

The discourse turns from the second-person pronoun, which would say "so you have no helper," to the explicit noun with the description "the wrongdoers," in order to convey the cause for the negation of a helper from them. So there is brevity in the speech, meaning: because you are wrongdoers, and the wrongdoers have no helper. The intended meaning is first the negation of a helper from them, and it is followed by generalization, negating a helper from everyone who is like them among the polytheists.

It may also be an independent statement, derived as a consequence of the story to which it is appended for the listeners, from His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved, for them is the Fire of Hell﴾ [Fatir: 36]. In that case there is no shift from explicit pronoun (*iḍmār*) to explicit noun (*iẓhār*), because the intended meaning is to convey that this ruling applies to every wrongdoer, so those who disbelieved, the ones being spoken of, are included in the generality.

*Al-ẓulm* (wrongdoing) is encroaching upon the right of one who holds a right. The greatest of it is polytheism, because it is an encroachment upon God by denying His essential attribute, which is oneness. The polytheist's encroachment upon himself, when he throws himself into punishment, is also of this kind. God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman: 13].

The generality of "the wrongdoers" and the generality of "helper" imply that supporting a wrongdoer is a transgression against the truth, because the truth is that a wrongdoer should have no helper. The wisdom and right of the matter require that the one who is able restrain the hand of every wrongdoer, because the community is obligated to repel corruption from its body.

[Page 321]

In this there is a refutation of the custom of the people of ignorance (*jāhiliyya*), who said of such matters, "Help your brother whether he is a wrongdoer or wronged." The Prophet (ﷺ) cast the refutation of this into the minds of his companions. He presented this proverb to them until they asked about it, then he corrected its meaning while keeping its wording, and said: "If he is a wrongdoer, you help him against himself by restraining him from his wrongdoing."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 35, verses 38–39:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾ ﴿It is He who made you successors upon the earth. So whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is upon himself. And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them, in the sight of their Lord, except in hatred. And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them except in loss.﴾

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that picks up from what came before) that connects the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing and Aware﴾ (Fatir: 31) with the sentence ﴿Say: Have you considered your partners whom you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth﴾ (Fatir: 40), and so on. Its meanings followed one another, and so he returned to summarizing the purpose that had been set aside, which runs from His saying ﴿And if they deny you, then those before them had denied﴾ (Fatir: 25) to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing and Aware﴾ (Fatir: 31). Thus the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ serves as a concluding clause (tadhyil, an appendix that confirms and completes the preceding statement) to the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing and Aware﴾ (Fatir: 31).

In this there is an allusion that Allah repays every person of intention according to what he conceals, so that the Prophet ﷺ may increase in certainty that Allah knows what the polytheists hide.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ is a new sentence which is like a conclusion (natija) to the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, because what is in the breasts is among the hidden matters. Therefore, from Allah's knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth it follows that He knows what is in the breasts of people.

Dhat al-sudur (lit. "possessor of the breasts") means the inner thoughts and intentions of people. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ in Surah al-Anfal.

In the announcement of Allah's knowledge of the unseen, the form of the active participle (ism al-fa'il, ʿalim) is used, while in the announcement of His knowledge of what is in the breasts, the intensive form (sighat al-mubalagha, ʿalim) is used. This is because the purpose of informing the addressees is to alert them that He is ... (page 322) ... a metonymy (kinaya, an expression in which the literal wording points to an implied meaning) for the impossibility that anything escape His knowledge. That in turn is a metonymy for the requital for it, so it is a symbolic metonymy (kinaya ramziyya).

The sentence ﴿It is He who made you successors upon the earth﴾ is a parenthetical clause (muʿtarida) between the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ and the sentence ﴿So whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is upon himself﴾.

Khala'if (successors) is the plural of khalifa, which is one who succeeds another in a matter that belonged to that other, as was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successor﴾ (al-Baqarah: 30) in Surah al-Baqarah. It may therefore mean that they succeeded nations that had passed, as in His saying ﴿Then We made you successors upon the earth after them﴾ (Yunus: 14) in Surah Yunus. In that case this is an explanation of His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the One who brought you into existence upon the earth, so how would He not know what is hidden in your hearts? As He said, ﴿Should not He know who created? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted﴾ (al-Mulk: 14). In this case the referent of the plural pronoun of the addressees includes believers and others among people.

It is also possible that the meaning is: He is the One who made you having authority over the earth, as in His saying ﴿and He will look upon how you act﴾ — ﴿and that He may establish you upon the earth, then He will see how you act﴾ (al-A'raf: 129). In that case the statement is good news to the Prophet ﷺ that Allah has decreed that the Muslims will become a people of authority upon the earth after nations that alternated in ruling the world, and that by this the religion of Islam will prevail over all religion.

The nominal sentence conveys a stronger affirmation of the ruling, which is Allah's making the addressees successors upon the earth.

Following His saying ﴿Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, there branches His saying ﴿So whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is upon himself﴾, and it is a conditional sentence used metonymically for not being concerned about their persistence in disbelief.

The sentence ﴿And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them, in the sight of their Lord, except in hatred﴾ explains the sentence ﴿So whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is upon himself﴾. The apparent sense of this meaning would require that it not be joined to it by a conjunction, since explanation is not conjoined to what it explains. But this was departed from to indicate concern with this explanation, so that it is made independent in aim of informing about it. Therefore it is conjoined to the explained sentence in its content, as a way of alerting to that independence. This purpose would be lost if the conjunction were dropped. As for what it conveys by way of explanation, that does not get lost, because it is required by the relation of the meaning of the second sentence to the meaning of the first.

(page 323) Al-maqt means hatred together with disgrace and humiliation. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Indeed, it was an immorality and hatred and an evil way﴾ (al-Nisa': 22) in Surah al-Nisa'. That is, the hatred of Allah toward them increases them. The hatred of Allah is a metaphor for its consequence, which is the withholding of His kindness from them and their being recompensed with the most severe punishment.

The structure of the sentence ﴿And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them, in the sight of their Lord, except in hatred﴾ is a remarkable construction, because its apparent meaning suggests that the disbelievers were hated by Allah before they disbelieved, and then when they disbelieved their disbelief increased them in hatred in His sight, whereas in fact disbelief is the cause of Allah's hatred toward them, and had they not disbelieved, Allah would not have hated them. The interpretation of the verse is therefore this: since they were described as disbelievers from the start, and then it was stated that their disbelief increases them in hatred, it is known that what is meant by their second disbelief is persistence in disbelief day after day. The polytheists used to act arrogantly toward the Muslims, oppose them, and cause them to despair of hoping that they would accept Islam, claiming that they were too great to follow them and that they would never abandon the religion of their fathers. They considered this to be hatred from them toward the Muslims. So Allah repaid them by increasing their hatred in proportion to the continuation of their disbelief. He said, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out to: The hatred of Allah toward you is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were being called to faith and you disbelieved﴾ (Ghafir: 10). That is, they will be called out in the place of gathering. The same is true for the meaning of His saying ﴿And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them except in loss﴾.

Al-khasar is the verbal noun of khasira, like al-khasara, and it means loss in trade. It is used metaphorically for the failure of an action. Their deeds in disbelief are likened to the deeds of a merchant who suffers a loss, that is, one whose goods do not sell well, so he sells for less than he bought them for, and so suffers loss. Thus the more he sells, the greater his loss grows, until it leads him to bankruptcy. This was discussed earlier in many verses, among them those in Surah al-Baqarah.
