Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 40:

﴿Say: "Have you considered your associates whom you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a partnership in the heavens? Or have We given them a Book so that they are upon clear proof from it? Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion."﴾ The discourse remained directed at addressing the Prophet ﷺ. And when mention had been made of the polytheists, their obstinacy, and their presumption that they had gained the upper hand over the Muslims, it returned to arguing against them concerning the invalidity of the divinity of their gods, on the basis that there is nothing on earth that anyone claims they created, nor anything in the heavens in which they have a share with Allah. So Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to dispute with them and to address the discourse to them regarding the negation of the attribute of divinity from their idols. This came after He had denied that they deserve worship, by stating that they do not provide sustenance for them, as at the beginning of the surah, and after Allah had established His control over the manifestations of atmospheric and terrestrial events and their varying conditions, from His saying ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾ [Fatir: 9], and reminded them of their own creation and the creation of their origin. Then, following that, He said ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion﴾ [Fatir: 13] and so on, returning to the invalidity of the divinity of the idols.

The argument is built upon the premise of observing the absence of the distinctive features of divinity in the idols, namely the exclusive ability to create existing things, and the absence of a transmitted proof, by way of the affirmative interrogative in His saying ﴿Have you considered your associates﴾, meaning: if you have seen them, then there is no way for you except to acknowledge that they have created nothing.

The thing whose seeing is asked about in such a construction, in usage, is the state of the seen object and the attachment of sight to it; that is, the matter of what is asked about is clear and evident to everyone who sees it, like His saying ﴿Have you considered the one who denies the Recompense? That is the one who repulses the orphan﴾ [al-Ma'un: 1] and His saying ﴿Have you considered this one whom You have honored over me? If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely control his descendants﴾ [al-Isra': 62], etc. Most often this serves as a preface to a statement that follows, which is like the evidence for it, or its clarification, or something similar, so its meaning is interpreted by what is connected to it of speech after it. Thus, in His saying here ﴿Have you considered your associates﴾ there is a preparation for requesting from them information about something their associates created, so the meaning of ﴿Have you considered your associates﴾ becomes: consider what you will tell me of the states of their creation of anything from the earth. Thus there occurs in ﴿Have you considered your associates﴾ a generality which His saying ﴿Show me what they have created from the earth﴾ details; so the clause ﴿Show me what they have created﴾ is a substitute for the clause ﴿Have you considered your associates﴾, a substitution of inclusion or a substitution of detail for a general statement.

By "the associates" is meant those whom they claimed to be partners of Allah in divinity; therefore the associates are attributed to the pronoun of the addressees, meaning: the associates in your view, since it is evident that the intention is not that the idols are partners with the addressees in anything; so the idafa (attribution) became purely in the sense of "those whom you claim to be partners of Allah."

The relative pronoun and its clause in His saying ﴿whom you invoke besides Allah﴾ serve to draw attention to the error in that invocation, like the saying of 'Abdah ibn al-Tabib:

"Indeed, those whom you see as your brothers, their resentment in their breasts is soothed only by your being struck down."

The indicator of the error is His following it with ﴿Show me what they have created from the earth﴾, for it is a command of incapacitation, since they cannot show anything created by the idols; so the incapacitating command is in effect a negation that they created anything at all, just as the statement in the verse of 'Abdah following the clause served as an indicator that the clause is for drawing attention to the error of the addressees.

The verb "to see" here is of the heart, in the sense of informing and reporting, meaning: inform me of a thing created by those you invoke besides Allah on the earth.

"Madha" (ماذا) is a compound word made of the interrogative "ma" and "dha" meaning "alladhi" (who/which), when it falls after an interrogative noun, and the verb of showing is suspended from acting on the second and third objects by the interrogative. The estimate: show me a thing they created from among what is in the earth.

"Min" (مِنَ) is for the beginning of the source, meaning a thing originating from the earth, or partitive, on the basis that by "the earth" is meant what is upon it, like the use of "the village" for its inhabitants in His saying ﴿and ask the village﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

"Am" (أمْ) is disjunctive, for a transitional turning away, and it indicates an interrogation after it. The meaning: "Rather, do they have a partnership in the heavens?"

"Shirk" (الشِّرْكُ), with a kasra on the shin, is a noun for a shared portion in the ownership of a thing.

The meaning: do they have a partnership with Allah in the dominion of the heavens and the disposition of their affairs, such as the movement of the stars, the alternation of night and day, the subjection of the winds, and the sending down of rain?

Since the seat of the idols is on the earth, it was likely that their imaginations would conjure for them complete control over the earth, so they were like earthly gods; and the claims and beliefs of the Arabs were varied fancies, mixed from the belief of the Sabians, the belief of the Persians, and the belief of the Romans, so they were like them; therefore it was said to their likes in associating partners ﴿Show me what they have created from the earth﴾, meaning: their control in that was the control of creating. As for the heavens, it scarcely occurred to the polytheists that the idols had any control over their affairs, and perhaps they did not claim that; but His saying ﴿or do they have a partnership in the heavens?﴾ came as a completion of the proof concerning the supposition and the possibility, as is said in the etiquette of inquiry, "If you say..." And they used to attribute to the idols a sonship to Allah, the Exalted, He said:

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾ [al-Najm: 20] ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ [al-Najm: 21] ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm: 22] ﴿They are but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

Therefore, on the side of argument, the negation of the idols' influence over the heavenly worlds was established by nullifying that they have any partnership in the heavens, because they do not claim for them, in their assertions, more than that.

When the due of rational proof was fulfilled regarding the negation of the divinity of those invoked besides Allah, it moved on to the negation of transmitted proof from Allah, the Exalted, establishing gods besides Him; because Allah is more knowing of His associates and rivals, if they existed. So He, the Exalted, said ﴿Or have We given them a Book so that they are upon clear proof from it?﴾ The meaning: rather, We have given them a Book in which they have a proof that clearly affirms the divinity of these alleged gods.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ʿalā bayyinātin" in the plural form. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, Hafs from 'Asim, and Ya'qub read "ʿalā bayyinatin" in the singular form. As for the reading of the plural, its basis is that the nature of a Book is to contain numerous rulings and repeated admonitions, so that the intended meaning of the giving of books of decisive indication is established, such that it admits no interpretation, exaggeration, or the like, in the manner of the scholars of legal theory's statement regarding the definitive indication of mass-transmitted reports. As for the reading of the singular, what is intended by it is the genus of proof, which encompasses many instances.

The description of the proofs or the proof as "from Him" (مِنهُ) indicates that what is intended is that the Book whose giving is supposed contains a proof for them establishing the divinity of the idols. It is not that any book they are given is a sign from Allah that He is pleased with them for what they are upon, like the indication of miracles for the truthfulness of the Messenger; the wonders do not speak to the fact that he is truthful. So the meaning is: We have given them a Book speaking like what We gave the Muslims, the Qur'an.

Then "Rather" (بَلْ) returned to refuting all of that, that all of it is negated, and that they have no motive for their false claims except that some of them promise others promises that are false, by which some of them deceive others.

By "those who promise them" is meant the leaders and chiefs of the polytheists, and by "those promised" their common folk and the ignorant masses.

Or it is intended that both groups are promisers and promised: among the leaders and imams of disbelief, they promise the common people the benefit of the idols, their intercession, their bringing them near to Allah, and their support, deceiving the common people; and the common people promise their leaders steadfastness in polytheism. Allah, the Exalted, said, relating about them: ﴿He had almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in them﴾ [al-Furqan: 42].

"In" (إنْ) is negating, and the exception is a branch from the genus of the promise, the object being deleted.

"Ghurur" is in the accusative as an attribute of the deleted noun in the accusative. The estimate: ﴿the wrongdoers promise one another﴾ a promise, except a promise of delusion.

The meaning of "ghurur" has already been explained at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196] in Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 41:

﴿Indeed, Allah holds back the heavens and the earth lest they cease [to exist or move from their places]. And if they were to cease, none could hold them back after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ This is a transition from negating that their partners have any creation or any share in governing the beings in the heavens and the earth, to affirming that He, exalted is He, is the Sustainer (al-Qayyum) over the heavens and the earth, so that they may endure as existing things. He, by His power, preserves the order of their continuance. This holding back is what is expressed in the science of the heavens (ʿilm al-hayʾa) as the system of gravitation, such that no defect afflicts it.

He expressed that preservation by "holding back" by way of figurative representation (al-tamthil).

The real meaning of "imsak" (holding back) is grasping a thing with the hand such that it does not slip away and does not scatter. So the state of preserving the order of the heavens and the earth is represented by the state of a thing's remaining stable when someone holds it in his hand. Since holding back carries the sense of prevention, the verb was made to govern the noun of cessation through "min" (from), and it was elided, as is the usual practice of prepositions with "an" and "anna" in most cases. This report was emphasized by the particle of emphasis in order to affirm its meaning, and to indicate that there is no laxity or exaggeration in it. This was already discussed at His words, exalted is He, ﴿And He holds back the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 65] in Surat al-Hajj. Then it was pointed out that the condition of contingent beings is to head toward cessation and transformation, even after long ages, so it was conjoined to it

Page 328
with His words ﴿And if they were to cease, none could hold them back after Him﴾. Thus the supposed cessation is also intended to mean the disruption of their order, which leads to their collision with one another.

Cessation (zawal) is applied to non-existence, and it is applied to moving from one place to another, and from it is the sun's decline from the middle of the sky. It was discussed at the end of Surat Ibrahim.

This verb was chosen over others because the intended meaning is the common one: Allah holds them back from being annihilated, and holds them back from their motion-system being altered, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outpace the day﴾ [Ya Sin: 40]. So Allah wills the continuation of the ordered motion of the stars and the earth upon this observed order, called the solar system. Likewise the order of the other stars beyond it, extending to the sphere of the fixed stars. That is, if Allah wills the extinction of those worlds or some of them, He will bring about in them the occurrences of defect, corruption, and rupture after cohesion, and parting after joining, so they will disintegrate and scatter to an end known only to Allah, exalted is He. At that point none other than Him can resist that or return them to their former order, so perhaps they will be annihilated, or some of them will be annihilated, and perhaps they will take new paths of continuance.

In this there is an awakening of insights, so that they may know that generally and reflect upon the coherence of this marvelous order.

The lam is an introductory lam for the oath. The condition and its answer are the thing sworn to, that is, the linking of the answer to the condition is affirmed and its occurrence at that condition is certain. The answer of the condition is the negated clause with "in" (negating particle), and it also stands in place of the answer of the oath.

Since it has been established by the preceding sentence that Allah holds them back from cessation, it is known that their supposed cessation can occur only by the will of Allah, exalted is He, to cease them; otherwise His holding them back from cessation would be invalidated.

The verb ﴿zalata﴾ was attributed to ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾ on the interpretation of "the heavens" as a single heaven. The cessation was attributed to both of them for the knowledge that Allah is the One who removes them, by His words ﴿Indeed, Allah holds back the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾.

In negating that anyone can hold them back, the particle "min" was used, emphasizing the negation, to specify the generality of the indefinite noun in the context of negation: that is, no one, whoever he may be, is able to hold them back or return them.

(And "min ba'dihi") is a qualifier of "ahad", and "min" is for the beginning of the source, that is, any one arising or existing from a time after Him. This is because the literal meaning of "ba'd" is the lateness of the time of "ahad" relative to the time of another, the one added to it by "ba'd". Here it is a metaphor for difference, by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), because the posteriority of the time added implies the difference of the possessor of that posteriority, as in His words ﴿So who can guide him after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23], that is, other than Allah. The pronoun added to "ba'd" refers to Allah.

This is like the use of "wara'" in the sense of "dun" (besides) or in the sense of "ghayr" (other than) also, in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"And there is no refuge for a man beyond Allah."

In mentioning the holding back of the heavens from cessation after extensive argument against the polytheists and denunciation of their delusion, there is an allusion that what they call to of atrocity is of such a nature as to shake the earths and bring the sky down in pieces, were it not that Allah willed their continuance for a wisdom, as in His words ﴿You have certainly brought a terrible thing. The heavens nearly rip apart from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 89]. This is an implication from the consequences of the structures, considering what provokes the contexts of speech with them, and it is also an allusion carrying a threat.

For this reason it was followed by a concluding phrase describing Allah, exalted is He, with forbearance and forgiveness, encompassing what the attribute "Forbearing" includes of His forbearance toward the believers in not troubling them with great calamities, and toward the polytheists by delaying their punishment, for delay is an effect of forbearance. What the attribute "Forgiving" requires, that in respite there is an excuse for the wrongdoers, perhaps they will return, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Perhaps Allah will bring forth from their loins one who worships Him," when he saw the angel of the mountains, who said to him: "If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them."

The verb "kana" (was), whose predicate is reported of the pronoun of Majesty, indicates the establishment of the attribution of the two beautiful attributes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 42 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 330]
﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if a warner came to them, they would surely be better guided than any (one) of the (other) nations. But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion, (in) arrogance in the land and evil plotting. And evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people.﴾ [Fatir: 42–43]

This is something the Qur'an relates about the polytheists, so it is the report of a statement that was certainly uttered by them. No report from the early generations (al-salaf) specifies the occasion of their saying this, nor who said it, except a statement transmitted from al-Dahhak, which is more fitting as an explanation of the pronoun in "they swore" and of the intended meaning of "from one of the nations," and he did not say that it was an occasion of revelation.

Many exegetes said: this statement was uttered by them before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ, when it reached them that the Jews and Christians had denied the messengers. What appears to me is that this statement was uttered by them in the course of debate or boasting between them and some of the People of the Book who came to them in Mecca, or whom they went to in their journeys to Yathrib or to the lands of al-Sham. Perhaps the people of those lands would call the polytheists to follow Judaism or Christianity and would belittle polytheism in their souls, so the polytheists did not dare to deny them, because they were held in esteem by them with the eye of dignity, since they preferred them for knowledge of religion and for not being unlettered (ummiyyun), while they refused to abandon the religion of polytheism. So they would excuse themselves by saying that the messenger of the people who invited them to their religion was not sent to the Arabs, and that if a messenger came to us we would be better guided than you, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or you should say: "If only the Book had been revealed to us, we would surely have been better guided than they."﴾ [al-An'am: 157]. The more apparent view is that those who invited them were the Christians, because calling to Christianity was among the distinguishing marks of the companions of 'Isa (peace be upon him), for they say that 'Isa instructed them to guide the children of Adam to the truth. The call to Christianity was widespread in the lands of the Arabs in the days of ignorance, and many tribes became Christian, such as Taghlib, Lakhm, Kalb and Najran. So this call, if the instruction of 'Isa (peace be upon him) to it is authentic, was a call of guidance to monotheism, not a call of legislation. And if this instruction is established, I see it only as a preparation for a religion whose call would encompass all of mankind; thus his instruction was a middle ground between the conditions of the earlier messengers, whose call was particular, and the condition of the general Muhammadan message for all people, in resolve.
[Page 331]
As for the Jews, they did not call people to Judaism, but they accepted whoever converted to it, as the Arabs of Yemen converted.

I reckon that the call to abandon the worship of idols, or to make known that they do not deserve worship, is not free of monotheist scholars, and on this basis it is possible that some of the advising rabbis of the Jews of Yathrib would present to the Quraysh, when they passed by Yathrib, that they were in error by associating partners with Allah, so they would excuse themselves with what is in this verse. It is parallel to His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And this is a Book which We have revealed, blessed, so follow it and fear Allah that you may receive mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 155] ﴿lest you should say: "The Book was only revealed to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study"﴾ [al-An'am: 156] ﴿or you should say: "If only the Book had been revealed to us, we would surely have been better guided than them." But there has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord, and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 157].

It thus becomes clear that this verse is linked to what precedes it of reports about the error of the polytheists concerning lordship, and concerning prophethood and religiosity, and that what is related in it is from their misguidance and recklessness.

Swearing among the people of ignorance was mostly by Allah, though they sometimes swore by idols, by their fathers and by their lives. The most common in this is that they would say: "By al-Lat and al-'Uzza," and for this reason it came in the hadith: "Whoever swears by al-Lat and al-'Uzza, let him say: There is no god but Allah," meaning whoever had that run on his tongue as a customary speech, and that was at the beginning of the spread of Islam.

"Jahd al-aymān" (the most emphatic of oaths): it is the most intense and strongest. Its origin is from jahd, which is fatigue; it is said: "such-and-such reached me to the point of jahd," meaning I did it until its doing reached my exhaustion, as a metaphor for the intensity of his resolve in the action. So "jahd al-aymān" here is a metaphor for their emphasis. A parallel to it occurred in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 53] in Surat al-'Uqud, and it occurred before in Surat al-An'am, Surat al-Nahl and Surat al-Nur.

"Jahd" is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object that specifies the kind, because it is an adjective of what should have been the absolute object, namely "aymanihim," since it is the plural of yamin, which is the oath. So it is synonymous with "aqsamu" (they swore). Its estimate is: "they swore by Allah an oath, a strenuous one," and it is an adjective of the verbal noun, added to what it qualifies.

The clause ﴿if a warner came to them﴾ etc. is an explanation of the clause "they swore," like His saying: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120], etc.

He expressed the messenger by "warner" (nadhir) because the disputation of the People of the Book with them involved threatening and warning, and for this reason He did not restrict it to the description of warner in His saying: ﴿lest you should say: "There came to us no bringer of good news or warner, but there has come to you a bringer of good news and a warner"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. This indicates that the disputation took place between them and some Christians, because most of the Gospel is warning.

"Ihda al-umam" means one nation among the nations that possess a religion. If they meant by it a known nation, either the Christian nation, or the Jewish nation, or the Sabians, then expressing it as "ihda" (one of) the nations is an ambiguity about it, which may be an ambiguity from the speech of the swearers, to avoid confronting that nation with an explicit preference over it, and it may be an ambiguity from the speech of the Qur'an, in accordance with the Qur'an's custom of disdaining what has no benefit in specifying it, since the intent is that they called Allah to witness that if a messenger came to them they would be the first of others in guidance, and when a messenger came to them they did not smell even a whiff of guidance. It is also possible that a group of the polytheists considered their oath by the guidance of the Jews, a group by the guidance of the Christians, and a group by the guidance of the Sabians, so the Qur'anic expression gathered all of that in His saying "from one of the nations," so that it accords with the statement of each group, with brevity.

The Kashshaf mentioned another view: that "ihda al-umam" means "the best of the nations," so it would be from the phrasing of the swearers, i.e., "more guided than the best of the nations." But he built it on an analogy with something that has no parallel, namely their saying "ihda al-ihad" (with kasra on the hamza and fatha on the ha') in "al-ihad," and the analogy is not complete, because their saying "ihda al-ihad" became like a proverb for magnifying a matter, whether in evil or good. The indication that magnification is intended is the attachment of "ihda" to a noun of its own word, so it does not require that it be a meaning intended when "ihda" is stripped of the attachment.

Between "ahda" (more guided) and "ihda" there is a deformed paronomasia (jinas muharraf).

This verse and others, and what is transmitted of the Christianization of some Arabs and of the extent to which some of them adhered to the hanif practice, indicate that they knew the messages of the messengers. As for what is related of them in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure when they said: "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being"﴾ [al-An'am: 91], that issued from them in contention and dispute when the proof bound them that the messengers before Muhammad ﷺ were human beings, and their conditions were the conditions of human beings, like His saying: ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20], so they resorted to denying that Allah reveals anything to a human being.

As for what is related of them here, it is their condition before the mission of Muhammad ﷺ.

"Nadhir" means one who warns by his speech. So the meaning: when a messenger came to them, namely Muhammad ﷺ, and no messenger had come to them before him, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Qasas: 46]. And this is other than the oath related in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it﴾ [al-An'am: 109].

"Al-ziyadah" (increase): its origin is growth and abundance in substances. It may also be used for strength in attributes, by way of metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿so it added to them filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. From here "ziyadah" is also applied to the change of one condition into another, or the alteration of one condition into something else, as in His saying: ﴿So We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 30].

It is also applied to what comes to a person of good, even if its kind was not previously with him, as in His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26], i.e., and a gift that adds to their good.

Since the coming of a messenger requires a change of the condition of those to whom he is sent into what is better, the assumption about them, when they made that oath, was that if the warner came to them they would be guided and would increase in good, if they were already in some state of good, for humankind is never free of an aspect of good, strong or weak. But when they became repelled from the religion that came to them.

The exception is detached from the omitted object of "zadahum": i.e., it added to them no welfare, condition, or the like, except aversion. So the exception in the phrase "except aversion" is an affirmation of a thing by what resembles its opposite, because they had not been averse before.

It is possible that the intended meaning is that when they swore: "If a warner came to us, we would surely be better guided," their condition was the condition of aversion from the call of the Christians to their religion, or from being admonished by the admonitions of the Jews regarding the reprehensibility of polytheism; so they swore that oath to escape the disputation, and what moved them to it was aversion from leaving polytheism. Then when the messenger came to them, it added nothing to them, but only increased their aversion. So the "increase" is in the sense of change, and the exception is an affirmation of a thing by what resembles its opposite. "Aversion" is their earlier aversion, so the meaning is: it added nothing to them, and their condition remained as it was.

The pronoun in "zadahum" refers either to the messenger or to the coming derived from "jaahum". Attributing the increase to it on both considerations is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the messenger or his coming is not himself the one who increases them, but is the cause of strengthening their aversion or of the continuation of their aversion.

"Istikbaran" (arrogance) is either a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "nufuran" (aversion), or an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), because aversion has the sense of a verb, so it is correct for it to govern the object of purpose. The estimate: they recoiled for the sake of arrogance in the land.

"Istikbar" is intense haughtiness; the sin and ta' in it are for intensification, like "istajaba."

"Al-ard" (the land): the homeland of the people, as in His saying: ﴿We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], i.e., our land. So the definiteness in "al-ard" is for a known reference. The meaning: they were arrogant among their people, refusing to follow one of themselves.

"Makr al-sayyi'" (evil plotting) is conjoined to "istikbaran" in the three aspects, and the idafa of "makr" to "al-sayyi'" is of the type of the described to its description, like "'isha' al-akhirah." Its origin: that they would plot the evil plot, by the indication of His saying: ﴿And evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43].

"Makr" is concealing harm, and it is evil because it derives from treachery, which is contrary to noble character. So describing it as evil is a clarifying description. Perhaps the indication that it is a clarifying description is what the idafa of the described to its description requires, to show the constant attachment of the description to the described. Hence He did not say "makran sayyi'an," and "he did not grant license for plotting except in war, since it is a matter in which such is practiced against its like," i.e., plotting against the warner and his followers, and this is blameworthy plotting, because it is repaying the one who brings about their good by concealing harm to him.

[Page 335]
It has been made clear that their lie in their oath was evident, when they said: "If a warner came to us, we would surely be better guided than them," and that they intended by it only to escape reproach.

The clause ﴿And evil plotting does not befall anyone except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43] is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) or an admonition (*maw'iza*). *Yahiq* means that something disagreeable descends upon a person and surrounds him, that is, it descends and encompasses him with harm. So its effect falls only upon its own people. There is an elided modifier here, the estimate being: "the harm of evil plotting" or "the evil of evil plotting," as indicated by the verb *yahiq*. If the definite article in *al-makr* is generic (*li-l-jins*), then by *ahlihi* ("its people") is meant every plotter. This is the most suitable reading for the placement of the clause and its purpose as a concluding statement, so that it covers every plot and every plotter, including those among the polytheists who plot against the Muslims. The restriction (*qasr*) in the clause is then an assertive restriction (*qasr idda'i*), based on disregarding the small harm that befalls the one plotted against, in comparison with what God has prepared for the plotter in His decree, namely the meeting of his recompense for his plotting. This is among the laws (*nawamis*) which the divine decree has established for the order of this world, because such harmful dealings lead to the loss of people's trust in one another. God built the order of this world upon people cooperating with one another, since man is social by nature (*madani bi-l-tab'*). So if individuals of humankind do not feel safe from one another, they become hostile to one another and hasten to harm and destroy, so that each one may triumph by the scheming of the other before the other schemes against him. This leads to great corruption in the world, and God does not love corruption. He does not inflict harm upon His servants except where His law permits something. For this reason it is said in the proverb: "No wrongdoer is left unafflicted except by a wrongdoer." The poet said:

"Every thing has a blight of its own kind, even iron is gnawed by the file."

How many laws in this world are overlooked! God Most High has said: ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 205]. In the *Kitab al-Zuhd* of Ibn al-Mubarak, with its chain of transmission, on the authority of al-Zuhri: "It has reached us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Do not plot, and do not assist a plotter, for God says: ﴿And evil plotting does not befall anyone except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43].'" And from the speech of the Arabs: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it headlong." And from the common speech of the people of Tunis: "O digger of a pit of evil, you dig only your own measure."

If the definite article in *al-makr* is the definite article of prior reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*), the meaning is: "this plotting does not befall anyone except its own people," namely those to whom the warner came but who increased in aversion. The placement of the clause ﴿And evil plotting does not befall anyone except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43] is then that of a threat: God repels their plotting from His Messenger (ﷺ), and the harm of their plotting befalls them, by His empowering His Messenger over them when they are heedless, as happened on the day of Badr and on the day of the Conquest. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54]. In this case the restriction is real (*qasr haqiqi*).

How many civilizational (*'umrani*) lessons, Qur'anic miracles, and hidden Prophetic miracles pour forth from this verse!

Know that the saying of God Most High ﴿And evil plotting does not befall anyone except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43] has been made, in the science of meanings (*'ilm al-ma'ani*), an example of speech which proceeds according to the method of equality (*musawa*), without brevity (*ijaz*) or elaboration (*itnab*). The first I have seen to cite this verse as an example of equality is the scholar al-Khatib al-Qazwini in *al-Idah* and in *Talkhis al-Miftah*, and it is something he added beyond what is in *al-Miftah*, where its author did not give any example of equality. I do not know from where al-Qazwini took it, since Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir did not mention brevity and elaboration in his book.

Since the author of *al-Miftah* stated that equality is the common usage of the average people, and that it is neither praised in the discipline of eloquence nor blamed, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that equality does not occur in eloquent speech, let alone inimitable speech. It is strange that the scholar al-Taftazani approved the words of the author of *Talkhis al-Miftah*. How can this be equality when it contains a clause with restriction, and restriction belongs to brevity, since it stands in place of two clauses: a clause affirming the intended meaning, and a clause negating it of anything else? The equality would be to say: "evil plotting befalls the plotters and not others," so whoever departs from that to the form of restriction has followed the path of brevity.

In it there is also an elided modifier, since the estimate is: "and the harm of evil plotting does not befall anyone except its own people." Moreover, in His saying *bi-ahlihi* there is brevity, since it substitutes for saying "by those who undertook it." The truth is that equality does not occur in the Qur'an; its occurrences are rather in people's conversations, in which no attention is paid to observing the rules of the language's refinement.

Hamzah alone recited *wa-makra al-sayyi'*, with the hamza (*al-hamza*) pronounced as silent in connected speech, treating connection as if it were a pause (*wasl majra al-waqf*).

[Page 336]

[p. 337]

﴿So do they await anything but the way of the earlier peoples? You will not find any change in the way of God, and you will not find any alteration in the way of God.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿So when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾ (Fatir 35:42), and so on.

It may also be a consequence of the clause ﴿And the evil scheme does not encompass anyone except its own planners﴾ on the second interpretation regarding the definition of "scheme" (makr) and the meaning of "its own planners" (ahlihi). That is, just as those before them schemed and their scheme encompassed them, so likewise will these.

Here "yanzuruna" (they look/await) derives from looking in the sense of expecting, as in the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*And disheveled ones who look toward Balal as thirsty ones look toward the rain-cloud's rain.*

Thus his word "ila" (toward) is a noun governed by a construct, and its singular is "ni'ma" (blessing), whose plural is "ala'" (favours).

The meaning of expecting here is that they anticipate what befell the deniers before them. So the inevitable descent of punishment upon them is compared, by way of metaphor (isti'ara), to a known thing awaited from them.

"Sunna" means custom or habit. "Al-awwalun" means the earlier nations who denied their messengers, as indicated by the context of the discourse. "Sunnata" is the object of "yanzuruna," and it is elided with a word omitted. Its implied sense is: "the like of" or "the measure of." This is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ (Yunus 10:102).

The "fa'" in His statement ﴿so you will not find any change in the way of God﴾ is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasiha, a fa' that makes an implicit condition explicit), because what precedes it, when it reminded people of God's way regarding the deniers, makes clear the constancy of God's ways in His creation.

The implied sense is: if they know this, then you will not find any change in the way of God. "Lan" is for emphasis of negation.

The address in "tajid" (you find) is non-specific, so it encompasses every addressee. By this the statement can circulate as a proverb. In this there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and a warning to the polytheists.

"Tabdil" means changing a thing, and it was discussed at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And do not substitute the bad with the good﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:2) in Surat al-Nisa'.

[p. 338]

"Tahwil" means moving a thing from one place to another, and it seems to be derived from "hawl," which means side.

The meaning is that honour does not fall in the place of punishment, and the punishment of the wrongdoer is not abandoned. On this meaning is the saying of the wise: "What is by nature does not fail, nor does it differ."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 35, verse 44:

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them, though they were greater than them in strength?﴾ It is conjoined to the clause ﴿Do they await anything but the way of the former peoples?﴾ [Fatir: 43], as an argument that their being equal to the former peoples warns that there will befall them what befell those, of the kind of what they witness of the traces of their annihilation in their dwellings.

The clause ﴿and they were greater than them in strength﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: their end was perdition, although they were stronger than these people, so that the annihilation of these people is nearer.

This circumstantial construction was used in this verse because of what the position of the hal conveys of evoking the image of that strength, for the sake of brevity, since the surah is about to close. For this reason, it was not expressed in its parallels with a circumstantial clause, but rather with a descriptive clause: in His saying in Surah Ghafir, ﴿Those before them, they were stronger than them in strength and in traces upon the earth﴾ [Ghafir: 21], and in Surah al-Rum, ﴿Those before them were stronger than them in strength and they tilled the earth﴾ [al-Rum: 9], where elaboration is preferred there by enumerating some manifestations of that strength.

* * *
﴿And Allah is not to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent.﴾
When He presented the description of the earlier nations as being stronger than the Quraysh, as an example of the former peoples, as a threat and preparation for receiving the like of their punishment, He followed this with a safeguard against the expectation of being saved from the like of their punishment, on the ground that they have means of salvation that the earlier nations did not have, such as their claim that they have gods who will protect them from the punishment of Allah by intercession or by repelling it. So it was said ﴿And Allah is not to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth﴾, meaning: suppose you are stronger than the former peoples and more cunning than them, or you have helpers they did not have, you still cannot escape the punishment of Allah, because nothing in the earth or in the heavens can frustrate Allah, as in His saying ﴿You cannot escape Him in the earth or in the heavens, and you have besides Allah no protector or helper﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22].

The lam of denial (lam al-juhud) was used with the negated kana to convey emphasis on the negation of everything that could come between Allah's power and His will. Thus this clause serves as a safeguard.

The meaning of yu'jizahu ("frustrate Him") is: to make Him incapable of achieving His purpose regarding it, so that any one of them escapes from Allah's intention concerning him.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ is a reason for the negation of anything that overcomes Allah's will, since Allah is of intense knowledge, encompassing everything, nothing hidden from Him, and of intense power.

These two attributes confine the impossibility that anything could frustrate Allah, because the incapacity of one who wills to achieve his will either has as its cause the obscurity of the place where the will is to be realized, and this contradicts the comprehensiveness of knowledge, or the inability to gain control over it, and this contradicts the generality of power.

[Page 340]

...and the Qur'an. Rather, the exact wording: "Were Allah to take people to account for what they earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature, but He defers them until an appointed term. So when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants" (Fatir 35:45). This is a reminder to them not to be deceived by the delay of the punishment, so that they do not take it as incapacity on Allah's part, or as His approval of what they are doing. They are the ones who said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment" (al-Anfal 8:32). Their knowledge that the punishment of Allah has appointed terms, determined by His wisdom, in which the welfare of other nations is preserved or generations yet to come are spared.

So "people" (al-nas) refers to the whole community, and the pronoun in "what they earned" and the pronoun in "defers them" refer back to "term" (ajal).

A parallel to this verse occurs earlier in Surah al-Nahl, up to His saying "when their term comes" (al-Nahl 16:61). However, in this verse the phrase is "for what they earned," whereas there it is "for their wrongdoing" (bi-zulmihim), because "what they earned" (ma kasabu) encompasses wrongdoing and other things. In Surah al-Nahl, "for their wrongdoing" was chosen because that verse came right after a severe denunciation of a great wrong they committed, namely burying their daughters alive. Moreover, there it says "upon it" (ʿalayha), whereas here it says "upon its back" (ʿala zahriha). This is a variation in expression (tafannun), which al-Ma'arri followed in his verse:

"If you wish, claim that those upon its back are your slaves, and call upon your god to bear witness, and he will bear witness."

The pronoun refers to the earth here and in the line of poetry, since it is known from the context. The word "back" (zahr) literally means the back of an animal, the part that shows of it, which is the part above the spine of the body and opposite to the belly. It was then applied to the back of a human too, even though it is not visible, because what is visible of a human is the chest and the belly. The "back of the earth" is a figurative use for its expanse, on which the creatures of the earth rest, by likening the earth to a ridden animal, in the manner of metaphor by implication (al-makniyya). Then this became common usage and turned into literal usage (haqiqa).

As for His saying here, "indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants," whereas there He said, "they cannot delay an hour nor advance it" (al-A'raf 7:34), this phrase here hints at the wisdom behind their being deferred until an appointed term. The implied meaning is: "So when their term comes, He will seize them for what they earned, for indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants," that is, Knowing during both the period of delay and the arrival of the term. For this reason, His saying "indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants" is an indicator of the response to "when" (idha), not its actual response, and therefore it is appropriate that it be joined with the fa' of causation (fa' al-tasabbub). As for what is in Surah al-Nahl, it is the actual response, and it is a threat that when their term comes, the punishment will befall them without any respite.

His saying "indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants" is also an answer to an implied question: What did the animals do that Allah should destroy them because of what people earned? And how could everyone on the earth perish, including believers and righteous people? So it is made clear that Allah is more knowing of His justice. As for the animals, they were created for the sake of humans, as He, may He be exalted, said: "It is He who created for you all that is on the earth" (al-Baqara 2:29). Their destruction may therefore be a warning to people, so that perhaps they will desist from their crimes. As for the condition of the believers at the time the disbelievers are destroyed, Allah knows best about them. Perhaps Allah will make a way for them to salvation, as He saved Hud and those with him, and perhaps if He destroys them, He will compensate them with a better abode, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then they will be resurrected according to their intentions."

[Page 341]

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Surah Ya-Sin.

This surah is named Ya-Sin after the two letters that occur at its beginning in the orthography of the Mushaf, because it alone has them, so they distinguish it from the rest of the surahs, and their pronunciation became a name for it. Its name was also transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abu Dawud related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite Ya-Sin over your dead." By this name al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi titled the sections on tafsir in their books.

Some of the early scholars called it "the heart of the Qur'an," on account of the description in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin." Al-Tirmidhi related it from Anas. This name is not well known.

I saw an eastern Mushaf copied in the year 1078 (AH), which I think was in non-Arab lands, that titled it "the Surah of Habib the Carpenter," who is the protagonist of the story: "And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running" (Ya-Sin 36:20), as will come. This is a strange name for which we know no chain of transmission. The copyist of that Mushaf did not differ from the familiar names of the surahs except in this surah and in Surah al-Tin, which he titled "the Surah of the Olive."

It is Meccan. Ibn 'Ataiyya reported agreement on this, saying: "Except that a group said that His saying, 'And We record what they have sent forward and their traces' (Ya-Sin 36:12), was revealed about the Banu Salama of the Ansar, when they wanted to abandon their homes and relocate near the Mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ). He said to them: 'Stay in your homes, your traces are recorded.' But the matter is not so, rather the verse was revealed in Mecca, but it was used as an argument against them in Medina." End of quotation.

[Page 342]

In the Sahih it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to them "And We record what they have sent forward and their traces." This interprets what is in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi in a way that gives the impression that it was revealed on that day.

It is the forty-first surah in the order of revelation according to the view of Jabir ibn Zayd, which al-Ja'bari relied upon. It was revealed after the surah "Say: It has been revealed" (al-Jinn) and before the surah al-Furqan.

Its verses are counted as eighty-two by the majority of the regional scholars, and as eighty-three by the Kufans.

Concerning its virtues, what al-Tirmidhi related from Anas is recorded: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Ya-Sin, Allah records for him by its recitation the reward of reciting the Qur'an ten times." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a strange hadith, and in its chain is Harun Abu Muhammad, an unknown shaykh. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: Its hadith is weak.

Themes of this surah

The challenge to the inimitability of the Qur'an through the disjointed letters, and the oath by the Qur'an, honouring it. Its description as Wise is incorporated to indicate that it has reached the highest degrees of firm precision. The purpose of all this is to establish the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) and to exalt the religion he brought, in a Book sent down from Allah to bring the community to its lofty goal, which is the rectitude of its affairs in this world and success in the eternal life. For this reason the religion is described as the straight path, as mentioned earlier in Surah al-Fatiha.

And the Qur'an is a call to rescue the Arabs, to whom no messenger had previously come. The absence of prior sending to them is a preparation of their souls to accept the religion, since there is no earlier preoccupation that would be hard for them to leave, nor are they content with what they already have of guidance.

It describes the aversion of most of them to receiving Islam, depicts their dreadful condition, and their deprivation of benefiting from the guidance of Islam. It also states that those who follow the religion of Islam are the people of awe, and this is the religion described as the straight path.

It sets forth an example for the two groups, those who follow and those who turn away, from among the people of the towns, through what happened before to the people of the town whose denial of the messengers resembled the denial of the Quraysh.

[Page 343]

And how the reward of those who turned away from its people was in this world, and the reward of those who followed was in the ranks of the Hereafter.

Then an example is set in a more general way, namely the generations who denied and were destroyed.

And a lament over the condition of people who waste the means of success, how they hasten to deny the messengers.

It arrives at reasoning for the nearness and affirmation of the Resurrection, sometimes independently and sometimes by digression.

It incorporates in its verses the expression of favour through the blessing that these verses contain.

It alludes to the indication of these verses and blessings toward the sole oneness of their Creator and Benefactor, in order to awaken them.

Then it reminds them of the greatest event that befell those who denied the messengers and clung to idols, among those to whom Noah was sent as a warner. Whoever denied perished, and whoever believed was saved.

Then the proofs of divine unity are brought, mixed with expressions of favour, to remind them of the duty of gratitude for blessings, through piety and good conduct, and of expecting the reward.

And the abandonment of polytheism, mockery of the Messenger, and the urging of the threat of punishment.

They were warned against its descent suddenly, when there is no possibility of remedy.

They were reminded of what Allah covenanted with them, of what He placed in their natural disposition of discernment.

And the reasoning for the enmity of Satan toward humankind.

And the following of those who call to good.

Then the reverse of the poetic device (ʿajz) was returned to the beginning (ṣadr), and it returned to declaring the Qur'an free from being a fabrication originating from a poet with the imaginings of poets.

Allah consoled His Messenger (ﷺ) that their speech should not grieve him, and that he has an example in Allah, since He created them and they disabled His power to bring them into existence a second time, yet they will return to Him.

[Page 344]

Thus the surah establishes the fundamental principles of the religion in the most eloquent and complete manner: the affirmation of the Message, the miraculous nature of the Qur'an, what is required in the attributes of the prophets, the affirmation of divine decree, the knowledge of Allah, the Gathering (ḥashr), the oneness of God, and gratitude to the Benefactor. These are the foundations of obedience in belief and action, and from them the Sharia branches out. It establishes the recompense for good and evil, together with the incorporation of proofs from the horizons and from the souls, with a wondrous variety. For this reason this surah deserves to be called "the heart of the Qur'an," because the arteries of the whole Qur'an branch out from its divisions, and its course converges upon its essence.

Al-Ghazali said: This is because the validity of faith depends on acknowledging the Gathering, and the Gathering is established in this surah in the most eloquent manner. Just as the Fatiha was named "the Mother of the Qur'an," since it comprises the foundations of reflection on its various parts, as the head is the origin of management of the affairs of the body.
